speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CANADIAN CENTENNIAL
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CELEBRATION PLANS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. I wonder whether the Prime Minister can bring the house up to date on the plans of the government for the celebration of the Canadian centennial, and whether any consideration is being given to the recommendation of the Canada Council that a national theatre should be constructed. I am certain that Canadians are interested in the very important plans that the government no doubt has under consideration.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: CANADIAN CENTENNIAL
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CELEBRATION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not at all sure that this is a proper question for the orders of the day. However, I realize the great importance of preparations being made for the celebration of Canada's centennial. Some months ago I referred to the question at length, for I believe that Canadians as a whole will expect that on the occasion of the celebration of the 100th anniversary of Canada's nationhood, the necessary plans in keeping with the importance of that occasion should be made far in advance. In so far as detailed consideration is concerned, there has been none as yet. There have been preliminary discussions and also a general review of the problems that must necessarily be considered in making those preparations which will assure that proper celebrations will be achieved.
In so far as the national theatre is concerned there have been suggestions in the past, and those suggestions have met with general approbation in the house, that artistic considerations and our national destiny demand that the fullest comprehension of Canada's artistic past as well as assurances for the future should be a matter of serious deliberation on the part of every level of government. I realize that there has been a suggestion-the hon. gentleman called it a recommendation-from the Canada Council, and that would be one of those matters which would be deserving of the most serious consideration on the part of the committees to be set up and those whose responsibility it will be to assure that the centenary celebration shall be in keeping with Canada's destiny.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): In view of the fact that these preparations will not likely become active for about three years or so, may I assure the Prime Minister that at that time we will be glad to associate the opposition with the full preparations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: CANADIAN CENTENNIAL
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CELEBRATION PLANS
speechtext:
I must say that I think Canadians as a whole would want to be so
associated, and I know the hon. gentleman would not want to be left out.

maintopic: SHIPPING
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PROVISION OF SERVICE TO UP-COAST COMMUNITIES
speechtext: As a result of the strike at the Northland Navigation Company there is, we are advised-and as undoubtedly the minister has been advised-[DOT] great discomfort because of the lack of supplies. speechtext: I immediately got in touch with the chairman of the maritime commission as soon as the strike went into effect. maintopic: SHIPPING

maintopic: SHIPPING

speechtext: The little people.

maintopic: SHIPPING

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: SHIPPING
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PROVISION OF SERVICE TO UP-COAST COMMUNITIES

maintopic: SHIPPING

maintopic: SHIPPING

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if on this quiet, pleasant morning the Minister of Finance would not take offence if I asked him a question. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OF CONFERENCE ON FISCAL MATTERS
speechtext: Replying in kind to this unusually inoffensive inquiry, I may say I do not quite know what the hon. gentleman refers to when he said I asked for a two-level conference, or two types of conferences. I must be very wary of these inoffensive questions of his.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OF CONFERENCE ON FISCAL MATTERS
speechtext: I can fully appreciate that the hon. gentleman's preoccupations are so heavy that he finds it difficult at the moment to understand a very simple question. The question I asked him was this. What reply did the hon. gentleman give to Premier Roblin who, when he asked for a full-fledged dominion-provincial conference, associated with that request a further request for an interim payment from the federal government to the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OF CONFERENCE ON FISCAL MATTERS
speechtext:
In answer to that now simplified interrogation may I say that the purpose of the several provinces which sought a plenary, negotiating dominion-provincial conference to obtain a variation in the terms of the existing agreements entered into in pursuance of the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act in order to derive larger sums under the terms of the agreements and the legislation. That was the purpose which was associated with the request for the calling of a plenary conference, and it was to these proposals that I indicated in


reply, as I have told the house and the hon. gentleman on several occasions, that obviously if that were the purpose there would be little point in calling such a conference unless the federal government was in a position to comply in some measure with the request for that kind of variation in the terms of the agreements.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OF CONFERENCE ON FISCAL MATTERS
speechtext: I will have to read what the hon. gentleman has said in such a complicated way with regard to such a simple question. May I ask him another question. Is it a fact that his seminar or study group has decided not to hold any sessions during the hot weather?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OF CONFERENCE ON FISCAL MATTERS

speechtext: I wonder if I could ask the Minister of Finance a factual question.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY
speechtext: Could the minister explain how it happens that the estimate of the payments to the province of Quebec under the tax-sharing arrangements act which he gave yesterday are almost precisely $8 million higher than the estimates printed in the blue book?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY
speechtext:
It is refreshing, for a change, to be asked what the hon. member calls a factual question, particularly after the type of question we have been listening to by the hon. gentleman from Essex East.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked a question on this subject yesterday, which will be found at page 5779 of Hansard, pertaining to the table of payments for the province of Quebec which I put on the record yesterday. His question asked for a comparison of the basis of those figures with respect to that one province with those given in the table which I placed on record in the budget speech as reported at page 2410 of Hansard of April 9.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that the table on page 2410 was based upon the blue book

of estimates which, as hon. members will appreciate, was prepared last autumn. The figures I gave yesterday were a projection of the budget estimates of revenue for the current fiscal year.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would now like to ask the minister a question which is not so factual. In view of the obvious reflection of buoyant revenues evidenced by this increase, does the minister not think the time has now arrived for the government to reach the conclusion that it should have a plenary conference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought 1 had made it clear on earlier occasions, at least to all other hon. members of the house, that the budget estimate, which included our forecast of the gross national product and our revenues, was based upon the considerations, including the expansion of the economy, that we found when the budget was submitted to the house on April 9. There had been a considerable change in conditions since the previous autumn, and those matters were largely taken into account in the anticipations for the current fiscal year, based upon the expansion of the economy that had already taken place up to April 9 and which we were then quite confident would continue at an increasing tempo. The expansion which has taken place in the economy since that time at an extraordinary rate had been largely foreseen then and had entered into our budget calculations.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY
speechtext: A further supplementary question. Does the minister still expect a substantial deficit?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY
speechtext: Order. I think hon. members should bear in mind that the estimates of the Department of Finance are still to be dealt with. There will be ample opportunity to debate federal-provincial relations at that time.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON PAYMENTS BY FEDERAL TREASURY

Mr. Chairman, when the clock struck ten last night I was dealing with the bridge which is being built over the Saskatchewan river in the city of Prince Albert, under the vote having to do with roads to resources. The city of Prince Albert is 150 miles away from the nearest resource road in the province of Saskatchewan. When I look at the explanation in the estimates book this is the kind of explanation I get: "Contributions to the provinces to assist in the development of roads leading to resources". I wonder how it could happen that the minister could say that Prince Albert is the southern terminus of this road leading to Uranium City or lake Athabasca. I think it is a way to divert the attention of members of the house.
I wonder why they took this means of providing for the building of this bridge under the roads to resources program. Any member who wants to know if a bridge is being built within a city or between two cities or between two provinces would never resort to the estimates of the northern affairs department to find that out. He would go straight to the Minister of Public Works. As I said last night, I do not object to the idea of the federal government participating in the construction of bridges, because it has been done in the past and will be done in the future. What I object to is the fact that this is being done by a department which is not supposed to act in this way. What I object to is the fact that when we vote certain moneys to help a certain department they take those moneys and use them somewhere else.
[Mr. Speaker/}

I do not know, as I said, if this was done by the minister just to be in the Prime Minister's good graces or if it is a fact that the master ordered the serf to act accordingly. But one thing I do know is that if the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, had asked Mr. Lesage to build a bridge in the city of Quebec on the ground that it was the terminus of a road to the resources in Ungava, where there is iron ore, the present Prime Minister would have been the first one to protest against such action and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources would have protested because Mr. St. Laurent had so asked or ordered.
I want to know today why the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources had to go through this strategy to cover up something which should have been handled openly through the Department of Public Works. Nobody in Canada will believe that Prince Albert is the terminus for a resources road to Uranium City. I also want to know if this is a new way by which the government can show political favouritism in the riding of the Prime Minister, by taking money from a department from which it should not be taken and spending it there to please the electors of that one riding. I do not believe that the Prime Minister of this country should have special privileges. I think he should be the last to ask for special privileges, and if the minister adopted this strategy just to please the Prime Minister then in my opinion he has not measured up to the high responsibilities he has in the government.
The minister should be man enough to resist the demands of the Prime Minister if they are not according to the rules and practices of the house. I want the minister to explain to members of the house and to the people generally why he has had recourse to such a means in order to try to cover up political favouritism for the Prime Minister of this country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could not quite understand the argument last night between the Leader of the Opposition and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources over permits, exploration leases and so on in the northern Arctic, because anyone who knows anything about the situation knows that the next great oil development could well be along the British Columbia coast. I have given a good deal of study to the program of the government for the development of the north. I think in most respects it is a very sound program. The development is pointed at the Mackenzie river valley which, as is well known, is probably the area of the north country with the most resources.

Sometimes I rather wish that a little more consideration with respect to development of resources would be given to the resources south of the 60th parallel. By far the greatest proportion of our undeveloped resources still lie south of the 60th parallel. I would be most happy if greater consideration could be given to the program of roads to resources in co-operation with the provinces. I have spoken before about what I think is a well merited roads to resources development in the northern section of Vancouver island, but I suppose because that is getting down toward the 49th parallel, and because it is along the coastal area, that project has not seemed to be considered worthy.
I was quite interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West with regard to the report on forestry made by the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. Having been a member of that committee, having attended most of the meetings, and having contributed somewhat to the preparation of the report, I was pleased that he approved of it. Of course that is only natural when you stop to realize that in the house he is considered to be the C.C.F. representative of the forest industries, and many people consider me as one who represents the British Columbia forest industry particularly. Therefore two capitalistic minds are bound to think the same.
I hope many of the recommendations in the report will be effected. I think they are sound recommendations. They are not new and have been made for years and years by most forestry and forest industry associations across Canada. By and large they are all very sound recommendations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder whether I could ask the hon. member a question. This is most unusual, but is this British Columbia member admitting that places other than British Columbia have made some good suggestions with respect to forestry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Kootenay West was complaining last night about his colleague muttering about him being parochially minded. I certainly am not parochially minded with regard to the forest industry and the forest problems of Canada. One of the recommendations has to do with the forest access roads program in co-operation with the provinces, which has been very well received. The committee recommended that the program be extended from eight months to twelve months, with a lesser share contributed by the federal government toward labour costs in the summer months; 40 per cent, I believe, and 60 per cent in the winter months. One of the reasons for this recommendation is that in a 66968-9-371
Supply-Northern Affairs great many parts of Canada, particularly British Columbia, it is almost impossible to build forest access roads in the winter. For that reason I heartily approve of that recommendation.
I should like to speak for a few minutes about the Columbia river. I have attempted in the past to get some figures from the department concerning the possible volume of timber that would have to be removed in the event that they proceed with the power development. I may be making a wild guess, but I know that country very well and in years gone by I have cruised timber there, and I would think there is perhaps somewhere in the neighbourhood of half a billion feet of timber in the area that may be flooded.
The point with which I am concerned is that this timber should not be removed without careful planning as to its disposal. The sudden dumping over a period of two or three years of hundreds of millions of feet of sawn lumber on the market, some of it of low grade, would have a disastrous effect on the lumber economy of British Columbia and Alberta as well. I trust that the Columbia river problem will soon be solved and we will be able to get ahead with this development.
I sometimes become a little concerned over the fact that we are not moving fast enough in British Columbia with the development of our power, and we may find in the years to come, if we fail to develop it early enough, that it has lost its value because of the progress in establishing thermal and nuclear plants which can be located in close proximity to markets and raw materials. By that time there may be a lessening in the differential between the cost of hydro power and other forms of energy. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that covers the remarks I wish to make at this moment. I have a few more remarks to make on the items.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the interests of saving time, I wonder whether I could ask the minister if he would like to reply at this time to the problem which has been raised by the hon. member for Hull in connection with the bridge, because if he did reply now he might save me from making a half hour speech.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
When the minister replies I wish he would reply also to this question. He could reply to both questions at once and that might save me from making a half hour speech as well on this subject. On May 8 the Prime Minister, in a speech at Montreal, had this to say:
Another 86.5 million acres on the continental shelf in the Arctic islands are now being developed under exploratory permits.

I emphasize those words, "under exploratory permits". On May 11, three days later, in this house the minister said, at pages 3514 and 3515 of Hansard:
-we have not issued any exploratory permits, as this article states, with regard to the Arctic islands and the continental shelf.
One of those statements is manifestly not true, and I think the minister should tell us which one is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad in a way that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has raised the question as precisely as he has this morning, because if it is true that I am not telling the truth, as the Leader of the Opposition said last night several times-I will just read his remarks. I was asked about these exploratory permits and the permits that were awaiting servicing, and the Leader of the Opposition said, "Just tell the truth." Later on I went on to say that at no time did the Prime Minister ever make a false statement and the Leader of the Oppositon said, "Read his speech." The implication there is that he did. Later on the same page of Hansard I was pointing out to the Leader of the Opposition that the thing he did not like about the operation was that it was so successful, and his answer was, "Why don't you tell the truth?"
Now we have the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate coming here and putting it down precisely that on May 8 the Prime Minister, at Montreal, used the figure of 86.5 million acres. I assume he is not quarrelling over the 86.5, because the figures change from day to day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No; it is the phrase, "under exploratory permits".

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He therefore wants me to explain "under exploratory permits".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not want you to explain it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was the one
who provided that information to the Prime Minister, because under these applications for exploratory permits work is being done. If you want to lay the blame on my shoulders for having put it forward in that way, I can only say that it was made quite clear in the house last night that work is being done under these applications for exploratory permits just the same as if the exploratory permits had been granted.
We have not the regulations ready for final approval by council; at least they are ready, but council is studying them now. If you want to quibble over that you can make me out to be in error. The Prime Minister


said "taken out", and there is development going on under these applications for exploratory permits.
As to the other statement I made in the house, at page 3514 of Hansard, I may say, as I made clear last night, that when you ask for precise terms there are actually no permits granted. An application for a permit has been received, priority has been established, and in the meantime for those companies which want it there are exploratory licences for them to go ahead. I made it clear last night that there are 10 or 12 companies actually doing preliminary work just the same as if they had exploratory permits. If the regulations are approved by council in the next week or so and the companies pick up their permits, as I am quite positive they will, there has been no time lost and we have been able to gain this year in exploration.
I am very unhappy that the opposition is trying to make a point of quibbling over phrases, but if you want to go out and say the minister was not too precise in using these phrases, then I am guilty. However, to say that I have not told the truth is going a little far, and I hope the hon. member will admit that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On that point, I did not say the minister had not told the truth. I did not say the Prime Minister had not told the truth. I said that one of those statements was manifestly untrue, and it is untrue. May I read them again. The Prime Minister said there were 86.5 million acres being developed under exploratory permits, not under applications but under exploratory permits. Then, three days later in this house, the minister says we have not issued any exploratory permits. It is not quibbling. One of those statements is a direct contradiction of the other. If the minister had had the advantage, like some of his colleagues on the treasury benches of sitting over here, he would have seen a great deal more made of a great deal less than this contradiction by the opposition to which his leader belonged, and by no one more than by the Prime Minister himself.
Now, I say this statement by the Prime Minister, which the minister has admitted is not correct, was certainly misleading to the public. The Prime Minister at that meeting in Montreal was trying to blow things up. I shall tell you something else he said at that meeting, since the subject has come up, which shows what a modest fellow the Prime Minister is. Here is what he said:
I have no hesitation in saying at this time that I believe that the government has accomplished more in those two years than any other government at any time in our history.

That is the modest claim the Prime Minister made at the Montreal meeting. That is one of the alleged facts that he produced to prove that. Then the minister three days later says there were no exploratory permits whatever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Work was still being done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Work was not being done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is another matter entirely. The Prime Minister has the responsibility to the public to inform the public accurately, carefully and precisely. No one was more assiduous than was the Prime Minister in trying to check up even the slightest deviation from technical accuracy on the part of his predecessors. He cannot expect and he is not entitled to any other treatment. Prime ministers even more than ministers should be careful of what they say and be sure that what they say is at all times accurate. This statement is inaccurate. It is preposterous. Imagine the Prime Minister saying in this modest fashion:
I have no hesitation in saying at this time that I believe that the government has accomplished more in those two years than any other government at any time in our history.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is accurate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes; that is accurate. It is true that he obtained more seats than any other government in history. It is true that he has a higher deficit than any other government has had in our peacetime history. It is true that he has spent more money than was ever spent before in our peace time history and-

I have only one sentence to utter on this statement; then I am coming back to the other point. I want to say that the Prime Minister who made this modest claim is the successor of a prime minister who in the first six months he was in office took this country into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and completed confederation with the union with Newfoundland. Then this government come along and say they have done more than any government in the history of this country; more than Macdonald, more than Borden. I am not surprised that he asserts he has done more than Bennett. But this is the kind of thing the Prime Minister goes about this country saying, and he bolsters it up with the statement that 86.5 million acres are under exploratory permits. Then the minister comes

Supply-Northern Affairs into the house and says, "We have not issued any exploratory permits".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister should resign.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is very difficult in the circumstances under which I am operating to decide what I should say. I know what the hon. gentleman thinks I should say.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If you want to get your estimates through, if I were you I would say nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I want to make it clear that I think we all appreciate that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has to put on quite a show to make up for the fact that his own leader made such a tragic blunder in this house a few months ago in misinforming the public over some very statistics that I put on the record. This whole dialectical demonstration by the Leader of the Opposition last night and by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is as phoney as anything can be.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As you are.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Any person of reason will accept my word that I provided the figure that he quoted from the Prime Minister's speech in Montreal. Whether it is an application for a permit which is waiting to be processed or whether it is a permit that has been processed, as far as the public are concerned they want to know only one thing and it is this. Is the development being done? I said yesterday, I thought very reasonably, that we had a right to take some pride in the fact that this area of the northern islands, where nothing had been done, had suddenly come to life in the last year or so. I think a political party has the right to take credit occasionally. This makes hon. members opposite angry because they have been brought up not with the theory of history that believes there is a right and a wrong, and not the theory of history that there is a scientific interpretation, or that God enters into this also. They have been brought up on the interpretation of the Sifton press that what is Liberal is blessed and that all those things that are not Liberal are the opposite.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is fairly close to the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I can understand why that is so, particularly with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He has done a fairly creditable job of making this a great big issue, but I think the people, as they see the development of the country going ahead, will measure this country in their own way. All these storms raised in the house are not for the purpose of getting
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

information but rather are for the purpose of making up for what they felt were the stings and arrows of events long since past. I am only here trying to present my estimates and I will answer any questions that hon. members put forward. But if there is going to be any blame attached in relation to this figure of 89.5 million-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is 86.5 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -or 86.5 million; it changes from day to day-and with the words "application for permit", whether "application" or "permit" is in order, put the blame on me where it belongs and not on anybody else.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not think that was actually the point of the hon. member's question. The question was as to which of these two statements was right. I will read the statement of the Prime Minister on May 8:
Another 86.5 million acres on the continental shelf and the Arctic islands are now being developed-
I think those are the important words in that statement. Last night the minister pointed out to the committee that 10-he now says, 10-out of over 30 applicants or people who have applied for permits in the Arctic islands are now doing active work. That was yesterday. Since the Prime Minister made that statement we are told in the committee on mines, forests and waters when considering the minister's estimates that no development work had been done up until, as I recall it, the end of the first week in June.
I think at that time the minister said this development work, or at least the beginning of it, was based on the approval by cabinet of new regulations for Arctic oil development. He said at that time, in the first week of June, that these regulations were before the cabinet for approval. I have continually asked him week after week, and yesterday I asked him, if these regulations had been approved, and the answer yesterday was "No".
As I said when I first stood up, the important point is that the Prime Minister has said that the Arctic islands are now being developed. Yesterday the minister said that 10 of the permittees who have some of this acreage are engaged in active development. This statement was made on May 11, and in June the minister said nothing was being done at that time, that things had to be held up until after the regulations were passed.
I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is quite justified in asking if this statement by the Prime Minister on May 8

was right, or whether the statement of the minister a few days later was right. From the evidence we heard in the committee on mines, forests and waters I would say that the minister's statement of May 11 was right and not the Prime Minister's statement of May 8.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the minister ready to make an announcement?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes. There has been a lot of excitement over the bridge, and I would like to point out that in the roads to resources program we have bridges in agreements with several provinces. In the first instance, under the roads to resources program there are bridges in New Brunswick and several in Newfoundland. I am not too sure about some of the other agreements, because they are not all here. There are bridges in Ontario, and also as part of the over-all agreement there is a special agreement to do a geological survey, which is an electromagnetic survey of the area, before we finally decide on the route of the road. Therefore in the roads to resources program the first point is that there are bridges and a special agreement on the geological survey. The bridge which is part of the agreement is not part of the issue.
The second suggestion made is that the bridge should be part of the public works program rather than part of the roads to resources program. We probably look on this a little differently from the way the hon. member for Hull does, because for years it has been the subject of great complaint in Saskatchewan that there is no way of getting across from the north side of the river to the south side of the river, and the geography at the present time forces you to come across the river at one of two places in that part of the province, namely at Prince Albert or at Nipawin. One of these roads, the Hanson lake road it is called, runs from a place near Flin Flon and works down between Nipawin and Prince Albert. The Uranium City road curves round through Uranium City right through one part of the province to Lac la Ronge, the final part of the route extending down to the city of Prince Albert.
We have maintained over the years in Saskatchewan-not just the Prime Minister, the people of Prince Albert but the province -that this bottleneck had to be eliminated, and for years there was quarrelling between the city and the province over who would build the road. One argued that it was outside the city and should be built as a highway, and the other argued that it was within the city and should be built by the city. But the whole thing was slowing down the development of the northern part of the province,
Supply-Northern Affairs and if we did not build this bridge there would always be this bottleneck.
I might say that this is not a new precedent. I believe when Mr. Mackenzie King was the prime minister of Canada and representing the people of Prince Albert he saw that a bridge was built south of there to make the Prince Albert national park more accessible to people from the south. That was a long way from the park, I would say the same kind of distance, but the people of that day were glad to get that help to funnel their trade and tourist traffic into the north, and they will be equally glad to get this help at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the minister has completely evaded the contention made in this committee on this matter. I first raised the matter when I spoke in the debate on the speech from the throne, and I am very pleased at the able manner in which the hon. member for Hull has presented his argument. Yet the minister completely evades the argument and offers no reply whatsoever.
The minister says there is a little excitement about this bridge. Naturally there is a little excitement about this bridge, because we need more bridges all over the Dominion of Canada and all communities are very excited about the federal government having announced, in effect, a new cost sharing program in the matter of building bridges. We are certainly anticipating that when we want to build a bridge across the Fraser river, or when we want to build a bridge across the Pitt river, or any other river in British Columbia, or when the people in Montreal need a new bridge, or the people in Ottawa, they can now expect the federal government to share the cost of that bridge.
The federal government has departed here from the old attitude toward cost sharing in the matter of bridges. The federal government hitherto would share the cost of the bridge if it was part of the trans-Canada highway. The federal government used to share part of the cost of a bridge if it was used over a river that separated two provinces. The federal government would share the cost of a bridge over navigable waters. However, any community bridge has had to be paid for, hitherto, either by the provincial or municipal governments or by the two of them together.
The minister rather surprised us, or I should say the Minister of Public Works rather surprised us, when some months ago in this house he first indicated that the bridge at Prince Albert came under the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We found it a little hard to believe our ears at the time. However, the minister said he had

Supply-Northern Affairs explained all this to the committee. He had explained to the committee last year how this bridge at Prince Albert happened to be a part of the roads to resources program.
As the minister's department knows by now, the minister did not explain to the committee how the bridge at Prince Albert was a part of the roads to resources program. We are hoping that the minister will now explain how a bridge 150 miles removed from the highway is a part of that highway. If that bridge is a part of the highway, what about all the other bridges south of Prince Albert down to the United States border? Cannot they also be said to be part of that highway?
We have need of a lot of bridges over the Fraser river, all of which would lead to some natural resource. There is hardly a bridge in Canada that does not lead to a natural resource, and the existence of which aids in the development of that resource. We are very happy that the people of Prince Albert are getting a new bridge. We hope this is the beginning of a new policy on the part of the federal government, and that henceforth any major community which is in need of a new bridge can apply to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and argue that it is within 150 miles or within 1,000 miles of a road he is already helping to build, and therefore the minister will agree to share the cost of building the bridge. We are very happy that the people of Saskatchewan are to be blessed with a new bridge. However, we do insist on an explanation as to how this bridge is part of a road the beginning of which is 150 miles away from the bridge. And how is it that the cost of this bridge is shared by the federal government through the agency of the department over which the minister presides rather than the Department of Public Works, which ordinarily is the department seized with the responsibility for matters of this kind?

speechtext:

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I hope the minister will answer the reasonable request of the hon. member for Hull and tell us how this bridge is part of that road.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Was that bridge in Saskatchewan not built by the Saskatchewan government under the roads to resources agreement signed at Ottawa?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That may be so. What we want to know is whether the corporation of the

district of Burnaby or the government of the province of Quebec or the government of Prince Edward Island or any other provincial or municipal government now has an invitation to go to the minister if it needs a bridge, and the minister will say "Let us see; there is a road somewhere in that area, within hundreds of miles of the proposed bridge. Therefore I am able to share the cost of building that bridge with you." If that is the new policy I welcome it, and I think the whole committee would welcome it. However, let us not have a situation where only one community in Canada, which happens to have particular representation in this House of Commons, is able to obtain a bridge which, so far as we can see, has nothing whatever to do with the roads to resources program while other communities in Canada are to be denied equal treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would you want us to dictate to the provincial governments where they should use the money provided for this roads to resources program by the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think I must tell the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that the answer to his question is yes; if a provincial government suggests to us that a bridge would play a vital part in the development of our resources I am certainly going to consider it. This proposal for a bridge at Prince Albert was not made by the federal government. It was made by a committee composed of several members of the Saskatchewan government, including also the mayor of Prince Albert, which argued that this was a very necessary part of clearing away this bottleneck into the northern part of Saskatchewan. We accepted that argument. It also happened to be near a road to a national park which, I think, was the earlier reason given.
With regard to the other matter which was raised, the government of New Brunswick asked us to bridge a gap at Fundy park which is not connected with another road-there is a gap of 20 miles-and we said, "Yes; it opens up facilities to tourists, and we accept it". So if a province wants to prove to us that the construction of a bridge is part of a resource development, we shall look into it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On that very point, the hon. member for Hull brought out very well yesterday that one of the most badly needed bridges anywhere in this country is right in sight of this very building, and not only is it near a national park but it is near a unique national park, one which was established in part as a memorial to those who died in the second world war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What happened when this government was in power for so long?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Same old story.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, it is not the same old story. I am telling you, you can look right out here and see the bridge-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Why not stand up and make your speech?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: All I can say is I have stood here all the spring listening to a windbag like this talk and not know what it is all about.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I listened, as I always do, to the hon. member for Cariboo, and there is no hon. member of the house for whom I have greater esteem. I do not take the slightest exception to what he has said, but I think I ought to reply to his argument, since I think it is a serious argument. He asked why we did not do anything about this bridge when we were in power. Well, we did not build a bridge at Prince Albert, either, because we did not have a roads to resources-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I will tell you this-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would you like to make your speech now?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Go right ahead. You would talk, anyway.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We did not have the kind of roads to resources program which the minister has before the committee now, because when we were in office we had full employment and did not have to think up schemes to keep the people of this country working. But since the minister has said he is building bridges anywhere within 150 miles of a national park to improve access to that park and other resources, here is a bridge which is within 10 miles of a national park and which is very badly needed, also, for the proper functioning of the government of Canada itself. It might be that if we had a good bridge across the Ottawa river, government employees could get to work at a reasonable time and not be delayed day after day. It might be we should not need to have as many civil servants and we could pay those we have better, as they should be paid. There are a variety of reasons.
I suggest that if this is to be the policy there is no place where it could be better applied than right here, and it might well be that if the minister would take the problem over from the national capital commission, which does not appear to be making much progress, under his roads to resources program, with his extraordinary capacity for persuading people he could see the premier
Supply-Northern Affairs of Quebec and the premier of Ontario and say "We will give you half the cost of this bridge", we might be a little nearer to getting the bridge. It seems to me that the hon. member for Hull made an unanswerable case for equal treatment with regard to that bridge, when he spoke in the discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: All I want to do is express the great pleasure of this group at the new policy which the minister has announced. If I understood the minister correctly, any municipality or province that needs a bridge-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Any province-I am sorry- the building of which would help to develop the national resources of Canada, then a request for aid from the federal government would receive very sympathetic consideration. I can assure the minister that our minister of highways in the province of British Columbia will not wait many hours before he will have a few proposals to make to the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: A point of order. You are doing a lot of talking about the minister of roads in British Columbia. That government has been trying, and sending out Mr. Gagliardi here, and he comes down here with a story and never does anything; just the same as you, chock full of b.s.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I regret that the hon. member for Cariboo is not as happy as I am about the new policy the minister has announced; because that new policy, if the minister really meant what he said and he will implement his answer and have some consideration given to these proposals, will mean more for our province than anything which a federal government has done for British Columbia for many a long year. We badly need several new bridges across the Fraser river, several new bridges across Burrard inlet, all of which would aid tremendously in the opening up of the resources of our province. I can assure the minister that not much time will pass before he will be asked to implement his words.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question. In view of the fact that the premier who is provincial treasurer of his province is going to wipe out the remains of the debt of that province; in view of the fact that they have a huge surplus and that the federal government is virtually bankrupt, does he think it is reasonable for the government of British Columbia to make those demands on this government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In answer to that question may I say that if the people of the province

Supply-Northern Affairs from which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate comes had the same faith in a high standard of living and in decent wages, then his province might also be in a satisfactory financial position.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Before the minister replies, may I ask him a question. Will he give consideration to the appointment of the member for Cariboo as his parliamentary assistant?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
All I am going to say to the hon. member for Essex East is, beware of caribou; they have sharp horns.
I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam kind of worked up a head of steam. I hope no one in the press gallery is going to take his word for that and say they are going to have all sorts of bridges in British Columbia, for the very simple reason that British Columbia signed the agreement and, like any province, will have to work under the terms of the agreement, which are a maximum of $15 million and in any one year a maximum of $1,500,000. If he wants to go back and say that this program is available under those terms, he should also tell the people of the province that British Columbia signed an agreement. Other provinces have agreed with us and with the program as indicated which provides for bridges already in their programs, and that is about as far as we can go at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: At the same time that the money was spent for the bridge in Prince Albert was any money being spent on roads to resources in other provinces over the $1,500,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, I think that is true because there are those under the special agreements-the same as the city and the province-the same as the special agreement we have in Ontario on the electronic, magnetic and ground surveys.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Any other province that entered into a special agreement would receive like treatment?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If they came within the terms of the agreement and the ceiling of the agreement, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are one or two comments I would like to make about the roads to resources program. After listening to the minister's opening, sort of freewheeling, all-embracing remarks, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who covered a wide range of subjects, perhaps we should classify the minister as the "minister of everything". He has certainly the fullest scope of matters under his jurisdiction, apparently.


I should like to make a comment or two, if I may, on the roads to resources program and the road which is being built in British Columbia, which is generally classified as the Stewart-Cassiar road. First, even though the contract has been signed with British Columbia on a 50-50 basis, I am sure this will also be the basis of the financial arrangement which will be entered into with the other provinces. It does not appear to me that the policies advocated or put into effect by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are in keeping with the policies of the government itself, because there is another department that participates with the provinces in the building of roads, namely the Department of Public Works.
I am thinking now of the trans-Canada highway arrangement under the Department of Public Works. Some time ago this department saw fit to make financial arrangements with provinces beyond the 50-50 program, and agreed to participate to the extent of 90 per cent of the cost of 10 per cent of the highway being built in a province. It would certainly seem to be sensible and in keeping with governmental policy for the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to adopt the same attitude, the same sort of approach when it begins suggesting that contracts be drawn up with the provinces with regard to the roads to resources program. If it is sensible to pay 90 per cent of the cost of 10 per cent of the trans-Canada highway in each province, then it is equally sensible to pay 90 per cent of the cost of the so-called roads to resources program in which the government is also participating. I think this is something the minister should keep in mind; it is something that he should advocate to his colleagues in an attempt to have government policy, in so far as participation in road-building programs is concerned, at least uniform.
I certainly hope the situation which existed on the Stewart-Cassiar road and which was fostered by a number of people out there will not occur in the other provinces, because it has meant quite a set-back in the progress that could have been made on the building of that particular road. As the minister will know, there was quite a bit of conflict of opinion as to just where the southern terminus of that road would be. Would it start around Alice Arm, or Terrace, or Hazelton, or some other place along the line? In those communities there was conflict as to just where the southern terminus would be.
Unfortunately this controversy about the southern terminus came at the time of an election campaign, and as a result every political party and every candidate got into the controversy and suggested that the southern

terminus for the road should be here, there and so on. All that the controversy did was to delay the actual program of construction of the southern end of the road. For instance -I am not imputing these words to the minister-I was told this and the story was quite widespread in Alice Arm. I was told by a person from there, who during the election campaign had been visiting relatives in Saskatchewan, that he had met the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and told him that he came from Alice Arm and that this place was one of the sites being considered for the southern terminus of the road. He spread the story that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources absolutely guaranteed to him that Alice Arm would be the southern terminus of the road that is being built up there.
This was an unfortunate incident. Whether the minister said that is beyond my knowledge. I am sure that when I finish the minister will take the opportunity to indicate whether he did or did not say that, or whether he recollects saying it, but the fact is that the story was spread pretty far and wide, in Alice Arm particularly and in other communities out there, and all it did was help to stir up more animosity among the communities as to which was going to be the southern terminus.
Unfortunately it had a bad effect not only in that way, but it had a bad effect on one of the communities in so far as its economic position was concerned, namely the village of Stewart, which is now to be the southern terminus of the road. The people of the village of Stewart had a pretty rough time last winter and the winter before because this government and the provincial government could not make up their minds as to where the southern terminus of the road was going to be. They would not make up their minds because an election campaign was in the offing, and if they made up their minds they might alienate some support in the village of Stewart and in one or two of the other communities.
I should like to pose some questions with respect to this roads to resources program. The minister says that British Columbia is the only province which has signed a contract on the basis of 50-50 financial participation. Other provinces have not yet signed agreements. It was our understanding originally that the contracts would be identical and there would not be differing provisions in the case of one province with respect to the arrangements with the federal government. It was our understanding that the contracts would be uniform. I should like the minister to indicate what the differences are and
Supply-Northern Affairs what is the reason for the delay in signing contracts with other provinces.
The $15 million is to be split equally between the province of British Columbia and the federal government, with each contributing $1,500,000 a year for a period of five years. In so far as the Stewart-Cassiar road is concerned, the rough estimates of people who have lived in the region for many years and of engineers who have surveyed the road indicates that the cost will be closer to $20 million than $15 million. This is common knowledge, and has been ever since this program started and ever since the provincial government participated, through its department of mines, in building a section of the road near Cassiar many years before the federal or provincial governments started to think in terms of a roads to resources program.
I should like an indication from the minister of what will happen if the contractual obligation of the federal government to pay half of $15 million will not fully meet the cost of completing the road. What will happen then? Will additional provision be made in order to complete the road?
We have heard quite a bit of discussion about oil and gas leases and the development of industry in the Arctic, the Northwest Territories and on the continental shelf. I am sure the minister has this in mind, but I hope he will keep in mind and carry out this general philosophy when it comes to entering into agreements to develop resources in the northern part of Canada. The history of industrial development and expansion throughout Canada has not been good. There are many cases on record where governments, provincial and federal, in past years entered into a fire sale of our natural resources in their haste to get some sort of development program under way. The Canadian Pacific Railway is a case in point, where acres and acres of land were given away. Forest management licences in British Columbia are another case in point. The proposed Wenner-Gren program would be nothing but another fire sale of our natural resources to outside private interests.
This is one thing the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources should guard against in his dealings with industrial people, particularly foreign and international concerns. He had better guard against entering into any sort of give-away program which will tie our children and our children's children to a contract which they cannot change in later years when some of them become members of parliament.
The minister has been referred to as a visionary. Of course I would classify him in the same way as the hon. member for

Supply-Northern Affairs Mackenzie River did the other day, when he quoted the dictionary definition of a visionary. The minister may be as dedicated and sincere as a person can be with respect to the development of our resources in the north. I do not question his sincerity, integrity or honesty in that regard but he should realize that neither he nor anyone else is infallible. We have no crystal ball in which we can see 30, 40 or 50 years ahead and determine whether what we do today will be acceptable and beneficial 50 years from now.
Experience has shown that past governments were not right in binding future generations to accept the give-away contracts into which they entered. We have found by sad experience in later years that previous governments were not so farsighted as they thought they were. We are now realizing the errors made by previous governments in attempting to have our natural resources developed and the production therefrom and the distribution of that production carried out in such a way as to be most beneficial to Canada and the citizens of other nations of the world. The minister must guard against that more than any other single thing. Do not be in any obscene haste, shall I say, to develop our natural resources. Do not give them away under conditions that bind the hands of the people of future generations, who may decide that the minister was not so clever after all, so that they will not be able to do anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to thank the hon. member for Skeena for being kind enough to verify my honesty and integrity. I appreciate it very much after what has been happening in the last couple of days.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I was not talking about statistical things.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, you are either on one side of the fence or the other.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As far as the
contracts with the provinces are concerned, we make a different arrangement with each province in order to fit the needs of that particular province. The province suggests the roads and we see that they meet our criteria. But with respect to all the legal provisions the agreements are identical. They follow the type of contract used in the case of the trans-Canada highway.
One new factor has come into the picture since last year which has affected the identical nature of the agreements with the provinces. That is the factor of time. The original proposal put forward by the federal government was that there would be a five-year

limit, and this was one of the causes for delay in getting agreements signed last fall. One of the provinces-Saskatchewan, as a matter of fact-took exception to the way the time payment clause would work out in effect. They asked for an extension of time. We asked the other provinces what they thought about it, and the final result was that we took out the five-year mandatory provision. You will find now that the new agreements run from five years to as high as eleven years, whatever is mutually agreeable between ourselves and the province.
The key clause to remember is that the maximum financial commitment by the federal government, agreed to earlier, is 50 per cent of $15 million over the period of time. With regard to the agreement with British Columbia, the provision of a maximum of $15 million is identical with the term that will be in the agreements with other provinces. If the estimate proves correct and the cost of the program is $20 million, then under the agreement the province has covenanted to complete the road, but there is no federal commitment to spend more than 50 per cent of $15 million during the life of the agreement.
With respect to the resources outside of the provinces, over which we have control, I can assure all hon. members that no person more than myself will seek every avenue to see that as much as possible these resources remain in the hands of Canadians or Canadian companies. I am not narrow in this matter at all. I welcome the setting up in Canada of subsidiaries of outside companies. I am very happy to welcome the interest of British, French, Swiss and Dutch capital at this time in our oil and gas resources.
I can assure the hon. member that I agree with him fully when he says that those in charge of resources have a great responsibility to remember that we hold these things in trust for future generations, and not to make commitments whereby we give away rights to our forests and mines for more than a reasonable period of time, and also to see that the terms of any agreement provide for renegotiation. I should not have used the word "mines" because there is a little different philosophy accepted in that regard. In so far as renewable resources are concerned, and even some that are not renewable, more and more we are thinking in terms of short term leases like 21 or 33 years than we are in terms of the perpetuity leases and these long leases of 200 or 300 years that used to be given occasionally.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We are very pleased to find that this particular department has grown rapidly over the past two years and that it is now engaged, in co-operation with the

provinces, in many fields which were previously provincial in nature. We feel that this could be a good thing; and if the program the minister has outlined is accepted by the provinces, then a great deal of good can accrue from the work of this department.
These facts, Mr. Chairman, make this department one of the most important in the government and make this one of the most extensive departments, and the responsibilities of the minister have grown since he took office. This will all be to the good, provided it is used in an advantageous manner.
I was very interested yesterday in listening to the remarks made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. One of the problems he mentioned was the tourist industry, and in recent years we have heard of some of the problems connected with that particular industry. A few years ago in northern Ontario we used to receive a great number of tourists from the United States, but the number has been dwindling in recent years. I think there are several reasons for this, and some of the most important ones were pointed out by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. These include the establishment of new and modern tourist camps, and making money available to tourist operators so they can bring the accommodation they offer up to the standard the people from the United States desire.
There was another point raised in the committee, I understand, by the hon. member for Calgary South. This related to the fact that for a number of years we in Canada have concentrated in our advertising on the fact that we are a wild, rough, frontier country; that the people from the United States should come over to Canada and rough it. I do not believe the United States tourists want to come to Canada to rough it. I do not want to rough it, as we are told to do in the various tourist pamphlets. We have become accustomed to certain standards of accommodation, and I do not think we want to be told that the Indians are running around in their native habitat and we are going to spend a couple of weeks with them and this will be fun.
I do not believe that is what really happens, but I think it is the impression that many United States tourists are given. As the hon. member for Calgary South said, we should impress upon them that we are a civilized country; that we do have shows and the things to which the United States tourists have become accustomed. Then the United States tourist would come into this country knowing full well that his wife would be able to get the accommodation and facilities that she wants.
At the same time, these United States tourists will continue to push further into
Supply-Northern Affairs the hinterland, where conditions are not as good as they could be, and this will bring more money into those areas and give the tourist operators an opportunity of improving the standard of accommodation they offer. Then the United States tourists will be quite pleased with their visits to Canada and will continue to push farther into the undeveloped areas, thus enjoying many of the things those areas have to offer.
I should like to mention, as an example, that conditions around Moosonee were relatively primitive until a few years ago. Tourist operators there have improved their facilities and are bringing in United States citizens by the thousands for duck hunting and fishing. Once these people come for a specialized reason, they will come back after they find that Canada is not a bad place. I would encourage the minister to ask his people to continue to press for the establishment of standards that the government could recommend for use in these brochures that are sent into the United States. Nothing is more disheartening than to go into a tourist camp which you may think is rated No. 1 or No. 2 and find that with regard to cleanliness and food it is not even up to the most elementary standards.
I should like to say a word now on the progress the minister is making in connection with these roads to resources. I find it difficult to understand why Premier Frost of Ontario, who has been talking about northern development for some time, has not negotiated a program for building a resource road from Kapuskasing to Moosonee, and one from the town of Cochrane to Moosonee. Both these roads would open up large timber and mining areas. If these projects were undertaken next winter they would alleviate a great deal of the serious unemployment that has been prevalent in that area. With the developments that are taking place there, power will be available, and I would suggest to the minister that he ask for the co-operation of Premier Frost in developing resource roads in that part of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
