speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Before lunch, Mr. Chairman, I was suggesting how this department had been extended and how the work of the department had increased. This gives me some hope that in northern Ontario we shall see

Supply-Northern Affairs something of the natural resources development that we know can and must take place and the follow up, which will be the secondary industry which will follow the development of our natural resources. To do this I would believe that we are going to have to have a focal point on the shores of James bay, the town now commonly known as Moosonee. The provincial government has been very much interested in this project. I know the minister is interested in it. It was discussed widely during the last election. The Conservative party during the last election, and in particular the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, made several references to a railway from the town of Churchill, Manitoba to Moose Factory and that this would provide, as the press release points out, a rail link between the two settlements, each of which is connected now by rail with the outside and to open a large portion of the coast of Hudson bay to exploration and development.
The minister also pointed out that they were willing to spend $36 million to start a survey for the planned railway extension and Ottawa would probably pay the whole shot. It went on to say what this will mean to the economy of the country. Over a number of years the Ontario Northland railway which runs a line from North Bay to the port of Moosonee has been very much interested in this matter. After conducting a number of surveys into that field they have ascertained the cost necessary to develop a deep sea port. They have done considerable work on it. On a number of occasions the premier of the province has indicated his willingness to spend upwards of $5 million on this port. I would suggest that the minister of northern affairs, if he believes in the development of the north, can find no better focal point than the port of Moosonee which will open up all of the Hudson bay area to further development. Much of this development has been curtailed for the simple reason that there is no port at the railhead at Moosonee and ships of any size are unable at the present time to come into the port. This is a sea port on salt water. It has a five-foot or six-foot tide and would open up to Ontario a second route competing only with the St. Lawrence seaway as a route to Europe and the markets of that area.
Mr. Frost, when asked about this matter, is reported in the Ottawa Journal of Friday, January 16,	1959-the heading is
"Frost 'Expects' Federal Government to Build Moosonee Harbour"-as follows:
Premier Frost has indicated he expects the federal government to build the harbour at Moosonee planned by the Ontario government.

He goes on to point out that the jurisdiction falls within the scope of the federal government. A great deal of work has been done in this particular field. There are a number of reasons that would make this a centre of attraction for a development port in that particular area. A great deal has been said about it politically, economically and otherwise in the last twenty or thirty years. The day is coming closer and closer where some of the objects and the need for attention in that particular area become more and more important.
Mr. Chairman, we should just like to point to the development that took place on the mid-Canada line. The great amount of material that was sent into that line came through the port at Moosonee. Many difficulties were encountered because of the fact that this was not a deep port, a port sufficient to handle boats having a draft that would be necessary to carry the freight they have in that area. But continually during the summer small boats ply that area carrying fuel, food and all the necessary equipment for the maintenance of that line. I think it is quite clear that if this port had been in effect in the days when they started to build the D.E.W. line the expense of transportation involved in the building of that line would have been much less.
The Moosonee area on the Moose river near the south-western tip of James bay has been a port for small ships since 1673 when the Hudson's Bay Company established Moose Fort as a trading post. It was customary in the early days for these ships, which though small were of considerable draught, to lie at anchor near the mouth of the river at what was known as Ship Hole. Cargoes were lightered from that point to the fort about fourteen miles up stream. With the extension of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway to Moosonee fourteen miles from the mouth of the river, the Hudson's Bay Company ships, all of small tonnage, loaded and discharged cargo at the railhead. In 1956 ships of much greater tonnage and up to nine feet in draught took on cargo at Moosonee. Depending entirely on its natural advantages, Moosonee has become a practicable rail to ship transfer point. With port facilities and remedial works it could become an ocean port of prime importance.
Interest in Moosonee as a port is aroused at this time because of the very extensive deposits of iron ore which during the last few years have been outlined and evaluated on the Belcher islands and inland a distance of 37 miles from Great Whale on the southwest coast of Hudson bay. These deposits are now definitely known to contain hundreds of millions of tons of good concentrating ore

ranging from 35 per cent to 45 per cent iron. While the Belchers have no source of power and would have to depend on imported fuel, the iron deposits in the Great Whale area have three potential sources of hydroelectric power within a radius of 22 miles. Neither location will present any great difficulty in establishing proper port facilities and Great Whale has a naturally well-protected harbour.
The advantages of a route through Moosonee for shipments to and from either of these points must be apparent to anyone at all familiar with James and Hudson bays. At best the northern route through Hudson strait is restricted to a three-month navigation period. It has been proposed, in connection with the shipment of ore from the Belchers, that this short period might best be utilized by establishing stock piles of ore at some ice-free winter port, possibly in Greenland. While this may be feasible, it does involve the expense of two extra handlings of the ore as well as very extensive docks and ore handling facilities at the chosen port.
A route to the south through Moosonee, on the other hand, would normally be open to shipping for a period of five months and under much less hazardous conditions than on the northern route. Stockpiling, if desirable, to extend deliveries to destinations over the entire year, could readily be effected at Moosonee and without the expense of building docks for this sole purpose. If this Canadian ore is to be shipped abroad to be smelted and manufactured for the benefit of a foreign country, there is little point in presenting the advantages of the southern route. If, however, the prevailing official and national opinion that Canadian ores should be processed for the benefit of Canada is to prevail, there is every argument in favour of the southern route.
Mining operations in remote areas can progress only if given transportation facilities which ensure prompt deliveries during the navigation season. Such deliveries could be made through Moosonee and by no other route. A return trip from Moosonee to the Belchers or to Great Whale could be made, with cargo in each direction, within a week or ten days. From Montreal by the all-water route two round trips during the navigation season are all that could be reasonably expected. It might further be pointed out that perishable foodstuffs, greatly to be desired in northern latitudes could readily be transported over the Moosonee route, whereas the all-water route would make this difficult and extremely expensive.
While the Moosonee route has the obvious advantages of a longer navigation season and
Supply-Northern Affairs is time saving, it also presents unique opportunity for additional savings. With hydroelectric power available from existing and potential sites on the Abitibi river, conversion of low grade iron ores to concentrates of 65 per cent iron content could readily be carried out. By using the natural gas which will be available in northern Ontario this year this process might be carried a step further, by a recently perfected process, to the production of pig iron directly from the ore. Such an advance would materially reduce the carrying charges over the railway portion of the route and at the same time establish a highly desirable industry with its consequential allyear round employment in northern Ontario.
It may be suggested that once the traffic in iron ore has been established the route would be of considerable advantage to the promotion of the development of other mineral deposits in northern areas. It would prove a direct incentive for intensive prospecting and development over a wide area with enduring possibilities. It could also be-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if that suggestion were put into practice there is no question in my mind that it would make a lot less effective many of the speeches of even the hon. member. It would prove a direct incentive for intensive prospecting and development over a wide area, which I am sure would add to the vision that the minister has seen in that particular area.
So much for the advantages of this rail and water route from the awakening northland to the heart of industrial Canada. It is a development which must be undertaken immediately. This proposed route has been suggested. Development work has been done by a number of people. Development work started in 1911 when the federal government, under E. C. Ells, undertook a survey of this area. Many surveys and many phases of development and potential development have been carried out since that time. On one occasion the navy was interested in this and an extensive survey was carried out. From these surveys it has been readily assumed that the work of dredging from Ship Sands to the port of Moosonee can be easily undertaken. Docks can be established on the shore to provide docking facilities. These can be built into the shore where there is quite a height of land. This can be done so that ice and other conditions which exist each spring will no longer be a hazard, and dredges can be put into that area as they have been in

Supply-Northern Affairs the past. It has been established that dredging work can be maintained, and that when the silt and the gravel at the bottom of the river is removed the natural flow of water itself will keep this port open.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is quite easy for all hon. members to understand what this can mean to northern Ontario. If we have a flow of traffic, whether it be ore going south or north into the European markets, secondary industry will obviously follow in that area to supply the needs of the mining communities which will be set up in the area of the Belcher islands. This development is absolutely essential in northern Ontario where mining, particularly gold, has reached its apex and no further developments have taken place in that field. We have large cities and communities which are completely dependent upon the natural resources they were built to supply and maintain, and as these industries decrease and the mines are worked out it is absolutely necessary for this department to supply the leadership necessary to develop secondary industries, and I suggest to the minister that this is probably one of the most effective ways.
Just as an added incentive, it has been established in the last few months that the work that is being done in northern defence in connection with the Bomarc missile site in North Bay will mean the installation in James bay of heavy radar equipment and communication equipment. I would suggest that this is an opportunity for the minister to put into force somethiing which will be much more effective than the $3 million his department is now spending at Father Point, Quebec, near Rimouski. If the department is in a position to build a port, which I suggest to the minister is probably very badly needed in the area, there is all the more incentive for the minister to give consideration, in conjunction with Premier Frost and the Ontario government, to the building of Ontario's first salt water port at Moosonee.
The result of this will be more than beneficial to northern Ontario, because it will mean a flow from the industrial part of Ontario through northern Ontario and into the European market. This route will establish a much faster and cheaper method of transporting goods into the northern parts of Europe. I suggest that if the minister takes a look at the vision of which he spoke, this port is much more important than building a railway from Churchill down to Moose Factory. We would much more appreciate a port so that we can go by water from Moosonee to Churchill. I think this port will give the minister all the added facilities that he would need if he wishes to

transfer some of the grain shipments from the port of Churchill to a port at Moosonee, where he would be able to take advantage of a shorter route from Winnipeg than we now enjoy.
For these reasons I suggest to the minister that he go into northern Ontario this summer to take a look at the facilities there, discuss with the premier of Ontario, who has made many statements about his willingness to co-operate and spend Ontario's money in this regard, and that the federal government give the leadership in the jurisdiction they have assumed. It will be very advantageous to northern Ontario, and I am sure it will give the impetus necessary to supply northern Ontario with secondary industries.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter I want to raise having to do with the general administration by the minister of the items voted to the department by parliament. The matter arises out of what has been said in the discussion of this item so far, and it has to do with his whole attitude concerning the administration and allocation of the funds voted by parliament. We heard the discussion about the Prince Albert bridge and we heard the extraordinary argument advanced that the contribution to that bridge was made under the item under the minister's jurisdiction No. 280 and under the corresponding item last year. Item 280 reads as follows:
Contributions to the provinces to assist in the development of roads leading to resources in accordance with agreements entered into by Canada and the provinces.
Two points arise from this. There is no specific reference to bridges, but I take it that bridges would be included under the item relating to roads; they are an integral part of a road system. I take that to be elementary. But the particular road with which we are concerned and in respect of which money was voted by parliament under the item I have just read is a road which, as I understand from the debate, starts 150 or 175 miles to the north of the bridge. It starts at Lac la Ronge and extends from there a considerable number of miles northward. In other words, there is a gap between the bridge in question and the roads to which parliament has authorized contributions to be made, a gap of some 150 miles. A road to the start of the authorized road is already in existence and, presumably, has been provided by the province and there was, of course, a bridge in existence which was serving that road. I take it the bridge with which we are now concerned is to be an

additional bridge in Prince Albert. It does seem to me that it is stretching the language used in the estimates unreasonably to interpret the expression "roads to resources" to include bridges which are some 150 miles away. It is not realistic at all.
While I have no doubt that the bridge is a very good bridge and that it is needed very badly, I am raising this other part of the question. Is the minister using funds which have been voted for a particular purpose set out by parliament for what appears to be another purpose altogether? Surely we are entitled to some better information and explanation than the minister has so far given us. If there is no better explanation, then, surely, proper legislative authority should be brought forward regularizing what has been done. Certainly nothing which the minister has said so far, either in this debate or in answer to questions which were put to him on earlier occasions when this matter was referred to, can be regarded as satisfactory. Something further will have to be done, either by way of enlarging on the answer given on those occasions or by way of an indication of an authority other than that which is to be found in the item which I have just read. Hon. members will see that there will be no control whatever over the use of funds voted under this item which deals with access roads leading to resources under agreements with the provinces, unless a stricter standard is adhered to. One could find examples which would reduce this whole situation to absurdity, in the light of the distance which the minister has gone today.
The point I wish to make is that the minister must apply the moneys voted by parliament for the purposes for which they were voted. They may not be used by the department under his direction in any way which seems desirable, no matter how laudable the purpose may be. No one who has listened to the discussion on this first item so far can fail to be alarmed, because not only had we this example but we had a rather extraordinary explanation and argument coming from the minister on another point when he was dealing with some statistical information he had given as to development permits for oil and gas when the hon. gentleman argued that development permits and applications were one and the same thing. Looseness of view of that kind, when applied to all these matters, could become serious.
One further question arises, and perhaps I may deal with this same item as an example. The minister, in his answer to questions on July 4 and July 6, concerning the roads to resources program gave some very strange
Supply-Northern Affairs answers indeed. If he would refer to a question asked on July 4 this session, as appears in Hansard on page 5469, he will find the following exchange-I will try to paraphrase the question and answer, but it is there for any hon. member to see who wishes to read it. The minister was asked about federal assistance for an extensive highway program in northern Manitoba, and in answer he said the province was already working on certain of the roads, but an agreement had not yet been signed. Then, in answer to a supplementary question, he said that the road about which inquiry had been made was a part of the roads to resources program. Then there was a question about the limit of the funds that could be spent, and the minister went on to explain the amount that could be provided. What concerns me with regard to this aspect of the question is that on July 6 the minister was asked which provinces had signed agreements dealing with the roads to resources program, to which the minister replied: "British Columbia". In other words, he made it abundantly clear that Manitoba had not yet signed such an agreement. I point out to the committee once again, that the item under discussion reads:
Contributions to provinces to assist in the development of roads leading to resources in accordance with agreements entered into by Canada and the provinces.
Observe that there is a definite limitation in that item. There must be an agreement between Canada and the province concerned. I should like to ask the minister to what extent has he been spending funds under this item prior to an agreement being reached and, if he has been spending moneys in this way as his answer would indicate, what is his authority for such expenditure? By what right has he spent this money, because not only must there be a vote-there is an interim supply vote-but there must be an agreement with the province. That limitation is imposed, and I think the minister would agree with me that this is a serious matter. If there is some authority of which I am not aware, I wish the minister would clear up this matter. If there is not, may I say to him that I regard it as a serious thing and something which ought to be clarified by the proper authority and regularized in the proper way, because if the minister will consider the other items in his estimates he would realize how far one could go in applying them if I am right in the facts as I have put them forward.
You can see how, for instance, under construction or acquisition of buildings and works, arising out of the reallocation of the town of Aklavik, item 279, the same principle

Supply-Northern Affairs could be applied to some other city in the country or area, and so on. One could give unlimited examples. I think the minister will agree, and I think all hon. members will agree, that the method of providing the funds through these estimates, with the approval of parliament, is a method that provides for a precise procedure. The bringing forward of these estimates by the government is not in the nature of giving the department a blank cheque. The expenditure cannot be defended merely on the grounds that it is a good expenditure in the circumstances. It must be defended as being within the authority granted by parliament. It is with that point in mind that I would like the minister to clear up these matters.

As I understand it, the legal authority for the vote


cannot be applied for unless the work is finished. No money has been spent under these votes because the money will not be paid until the agreement is signed. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is precisely my point. Then some money was paid before there was legal authority. What protection is there? I want to make myself perfectly clear in this. I pointed it out to the minister and he undertook to have the point looked into. Then the debate today and last night on this same point rather alarmed me. In addition to the two instances I have mentioned the minister has said that there was an expenditure made in Saskatchewan, although there is no agreement with Saskatchewan. I wonder whether the minister will have this whole practice looked at and get a legal opinion on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

It was discussed by the officials of treasury board, with full treasury board, and it was agreed upon. I shall be glad to look into it again.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

I hope the minister will not find me too persistent when I say I do not find the treasury board infallible. I find it tending to be used very often as an excuse and sometimes blamed for a great many things. I still think that parliamentary control is the last word in these matters of voting the taxpayers' money and must be preserved as the last word. The mere fact that treasury board said it is all right to do it may be the beginning of a very bad practice. I hope that he will not be too

Mr. Chairman, this whole question of roads to resources is something which is very close to the hearts of my constituents in northern Alberta. I am very pleased to see that there is some hope that the mines committee may go north, and I hope that they will look into the northern half of Alberta while they are touring the north country because the transportation facilities up there are just about unbelievable. McMurray and Waterways are 150 miles from the nearest road, and our province is so vast that it is apparently outside the ability of the provincial legislature to build roads into those outlying communities where the population is small but the need is great.
I am only too pleased to see that the policy of the northern affairs department is flexible enough to provide such things as access bridges which make it possible to get onto what roads they do have in the north country.
We have another bottleneck apart from the physical bottleneck and that is the political one. The government of Alberta refuses to build roads into the north for reasons perhaps best known to themselves. I represent this great northern community but it is very difficult for me to get transportation facilities into those northern districts without emphasizing the needs to the northern affairs department in the hope that the roads to resources program may give them the only hope they have for a road. This also has a bearing on the question of building a railway up through my constituency. I have been accused at times of not pressing this railway as vigorously as I should. This is not the point. A good road into McMurray and Waterways would drastically reduce freight rates into the north and this would speed up the development of the whole of the north country from McMurray and Waterways right clean down to the Mackenzie delta and the whole of the Canadian shield. It is my considered opinion that a good all-weather road north between Edmonton and McMurray would do more to reduce freight costs in that whole country than anything else we could do. It may be significant that the only Liberal member returned in Alberta was from a provincial riding in my district where he has made himself vocal about transportation. These people, desperate as they are for transportation, saw fit to return a Liberal member to the legislature.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I think I should take this occasion to compliment the minister at least on his industry and zeal. I cannot agree that he always makes the right moves, but then there is the old story that the only man who does not make a mistake is the man who does not do anything. Certainly I think the minister has shown considerable industry and zeal in the pursuit of his duties in the department.
I should also like to say that I think the standing committee on mines, forests and waters did an outstanding job both this year and last year in dealing with the estimates of the department. I think their actions have been an example that many of the other committees could follow.
This department deals with the far north and I prefer that description because the riding I represent has been known for many years as the "north" and we have always considered ourselves as such. When this new great northern vision came along in the last federal election the people of northern Ontario more or less got the feeling that they were being by-passed, that they were no longer the north. I do not know whether you would call that area the near north, but it seemed that all the direction and energy of the federal government with regard to this vision was concentrated on the far north and by-passed the northern part of Ontario.
Of course, it is true that the government has continued, as the former government did, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and has increased the assistance under that legislation. But many people, particularly in my riding, which possibly is affected as much as any riding in Canada by this legislation, have thought for a long time that rather than subsidizing these gold mines there might be other methods of using this money that would better implement the original intention of the legislation, that is, the maintenance and development of the mining municipalities of northern Ontario. That is why I was so pleased today, along with the hon. member

Supply-Northern Affairs for Burnaby-Coquitlam, to hear the new policy announced by the minister. I think that the municipalities in the area I represent will certainly be very pleased to know that any assistance along this line may not necessarily be confined to more northerly regions and that if a case can be prepared justifying local assistance it will receive favourable consideration similar to that extended to Prince Albert, Saskatchewan.
However, Mr. Chairman, I think I should warn the minister at this stage that if any bridges are going to be built in northern Ontario he should keep a very close eye on them. We have learned from bitter experience in the past that bridges in northern Ontario by the Ontario government have a habit of disappearing and that although you may pay for them you are never able to find them. I suggest that if the construction of any bridges is embarked upon in this area the minister and his officials should keep a very close eye on them. Any assistance along this line will certainly be a terrific boon to the area I represent.
One thing that the area has needed for many years has been the opportunity to participate in the tourist industry but the industry has always fallen a little short of reaching our area. We are very hopeful that this situation can be corrected in the not too distant future. Certainly any consideration that the minister and his department can give to assistance along this line will be very much appreciated. We have all watched with some interest the recent development whereby the town of Timmins, which for many years has been known for its production of gold, suddenly became internationally known over night for its production of bears. I am sure that in the future that will stimulate the interest of many tourists in the area.
I should also like to endorse heartily the remarks of the hon. member for Timiska-ming with regard to a port at Moosonee. If this very worth-while project is carried out the area I represent will no longer be the end of the line as it has been in the past. I think that possibly one of the greatest drawbacks to the establishment of secondary industries has been the fact that the area was the end of the line, and if the project to establish a salt water port at Moosonee is ever embarked upon it will have very beneficial effects.
Possibly one of the biggest shadows hanging over any mining municipality is the fact that the gold, or whatever the mineral is, is an expendable resource. There is always hanging over people's heads the thought that some day, be it ten years or fifty years from now, the ore will be exhausted in the area and, of course, that creates a sense of urgency

with respect to the need for other industries and occupations to take up the slack which inevitably will come. Any development of the port or of the area leading up to the port of Moosonee will lead to new mineral exploration so that the secondary industries may very well be new mineral projects.
I should also like to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena when he warned the minister to guard rather carefully our resources which, to use the minister's own words, we hold in trust for future generations. In today's Globe and Mail I noticed something which bears this out very well. I do not know whether hon. members have read this article on page 7 of today's paper. It deals with the big nickel development in northern Manitoba. It is a fantastic story, one which most people would never even dream could happen in Canada today. I should like to put a few excerpts from the article on Hansard. It deals, of course, with the giant company that put up $175 million to develop this resource in northern Manitoba.
The provincial government was so delighted to see this new industry established that they leaped before they thought. They tied themselves up under agreements and it did not take very long for them to rue the day. In fact, I believe even before the industry had gone into production they were finding, to their grief, they should have been a little more careful before they signed this agreement. The article deals with a member of the provincial legislature who wanted to go into the area to see what was transpiring in this new municipality of Thompson in northern Manitoba. Here is what happened, and I shall read from this article:
He telephoned Inco at Winnipeg.
This was to procure a train ticket to go into this area. He was told no by a company executive.
Mr. Orlikow could not go to Thompson: There wasn't room for him there. Under the agreements the company owned everything. The railways could not even sell a ticket into Thompson, except to persons with a company pass.
Of course Mr. Orlikow, the provincial M.L.A., did not possess this pass. Then, when he decided to go in anyway, according to this article, he found that he could not rent a room because all the buildings were owned by the company and the people did not feel free to rent him a room. So he wanted to know if he could buy a tent and camp in the town.
The article reads:
No, the town's zoning regulations prevented camping. Could he camp across the river from the town? No, under the agreements, the town controlled all such practices in the vicinity, even though, of course, it was crown land.

Then farther down on the page we find this:
Provincial officers went to Thompson to arrange a poll in the provincial election. No, said the company, there could be no poll on company property. It had to be a mile away. The result: 50 of Thompson's 1,000 voters cast ballots. A new inquiry has been started by the municipal affairs department to see what the election act has to say about that.
This illustrates very clearly the point raised by the hon. member for Skeena this morning to the effect that great care must be taken, and we must not leap in too quickly in signing agreements which could lead to situations such as this. The hon. member for Skeena mentioned what may happen 50 or 100 years from now, but here we have an example of what happens a few years after such an agreement is signed. In fact, the closing paragraph of this article poses a very significant question:
The question government lawyers want to answer: Just how much can you buy with $175 million?
So, Mr. Chairman, I would once again say how much we welcome the new policy the minister announced this morning. However, there is one thought that occurs to me. I understand that one province has already signed an agreement with the federal government with regard to these roads to resources. Now we find a new policy has been announced from that which I imagine was on the table during the discussions with the province that has already signed. I think this may hinder or further delay the signing of agreements with other provinces because when they see this change they will hope that there may be further changes in the future, and this could lead to considerable delay of this worth-while project in connection with roads to resources.

Mr. Chairman, I was
wondering, too, whether perhaps the transaction could be summarized in another way. Perhaps this bridge was not so much for access to natural resources as for the conservation of political resources. Supply-Northern Affairs department. I should like to quote from paragraph 24 of the report of the committee:
It became clear during the examination of the estimates of the northern administrative branch that the government policy in the north over many years has been a vacillation between inaction and reaction-inaction in not doing the things that obviously were required to be done, and reaction in doing things only when we were pushed into them by the activities of other countries.
Mr. Chairman, during the committee hearings in this particular regard the total evidence can be found on pages 467 to 470, inclusive, and this evidence is the evidence of one witness. Only one witness was called before this committee, namely Mr. Rowley, the chief of the northern co-ordination centre. In any event, the first part of paragraph 24 is apparently substantiated by questions and answers in the proceedings of the mines, forests and waters committee at page 467, which read as follows:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Rowley, would I be correct in saying that policy in the past has been a mixture or perhaps a vacillation between inaction and reaction-inaction in not doing the things that obviously had to be done and reaction in doing things only when we are pushed into them by the activities of other countries.
This was the first question asked Mr. Rowley. Not one bit of evidence had come before the committee at that time. I ask members of this committee, is this a question, or is this an observation by the hon. member for Yukon that is based on any evidence? In any event, Mr. Rowley answered as follows:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I think it is a fair statement that most of the research which we have carried out was initiated and appears to have been inspired by outside influence-by a fear that other people would do it, or an obvious need to keep up with one's neighbours.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You mean other countries, Mr. Rowley? You mentioned "other people"; you mean other countries?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes. largely other countries.
This is all the evidence that was taken in this committee on mines, forests and waters on which to base this part of the report. The wording is entirely the wording of the hon. member for Yukon in an observation he made in the form of a question. The next sentence in the report of the committee says:
Judging from what has been done in Canada's north the government policy has fallen far short of being adequate in almost every aspect of research. Where Canada should have been a leading nation in northern research we have fallen behind. Improvements in recent years have been made, but much too slowly.
We will go back to the evidence before the committee, Mr. Chairman, and we will find that this statement is apparently substantiated by evidence which appears on page 467 of the committee proceedings, a

Supply-Northern Affairs question by the hon. member for Yukon to Mr. Rowley, which reads as follows:
If this is not too sweeping a question to ask you, Mr. Rowley, just what do you conceive to be Canada's responsibility as a polar nation; first, in so far as resource development is concerned- well, let us stick to the item, in so far as scientific research is concerned for the area north of the 60th parallel?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, I think, Mr. Chairman, that it is quite obvious we have a large core of the Arctic region, and with our possession of that part goes the responsibility of carrying out a full program of research. As we have a very large part, I think we should be a leading nation in so far as research in the Arctic is concerned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Have we been a leading nation in this field for the past 10 years?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, we have not been a leading nation. I think we have been improving our position. We have been doing more since the war. We have been increasing the amount we have been doing, but we started from virtually nothing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What in your view would be the reason for not taking the lead in this research: would it be a lack of funds, a lack of attention, or what would it be?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Of course, it has been a lack of funds and a lack of people; but I think one must remember in saying this, that it is a particularly large country with a comparatively small population, and the demands of the rest of the country are very pressing, which has had the effect of putting research in the north in the background. There are so many things more pressing, more immediate, and more obviously of practical importance that research in the north would sometimes fall behind.
Now, this portion of the evidence seeks to substantiate the sweeping statement in the recommendation of the committee. On the rest of the page there is a question about Mr. Rowley ever having been in the Arctic, and he had been. Then I find the following on page 468 of the proceedings of the committee:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Are you familiar with Captain
Joseph Bernier's work in the Arctic years ago?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, I am familiar with that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I believe he died in 1934. Do you feel we have made any substantial progress in our Arctic areas, since the death of Captain Bernier, along the lines on which he was thinking?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, we have made substantial progress, Mr. Chairman. Captain Bernier really was carrying out exploration and he was the end, in many ways, of one phase. He really came into it too late, because most of the original exploration had been carried out by the time he came along. This exploration has taken a different form since: it is a scientific exploration, dealing with the details of various scientific disciplines, rather than finding out where the land and water lie. Since then we have done quite a lot, and I think the geological survey particularly has been the most active agency in the government in this respect.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Do you find you are restricted in the department with what you want to do or what you feel we should be doing in the Arctic because of restrictions placed on other departments, because of inability to obtain information from other departments such as that of mines and technical surveys?
[Mr. Hardie.'i

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Do you mean so far as development is concerned and not so far as research is concerned?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Scientific research.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, I think we are. All scientific research depends on basic scientific data and there is a great shortage of basic facts about the Arctic. I think this goes into all phases of research and it affects all development, either resource development or social development. We do not know enough facts. In the case of resource development, I think to some extent it is rather better because they are well established and have extremely effective agencies gathering facts. They are not gathering them as fast as we would like, but certainly this collection of scientific data is going on.
Then, section 25 of the report of the committee reads as follows:
There are insufficient field laboratories in Canada's northland to accomplish adequate research. Small research laboratories or stations established in various northern localities are essential if we are to discharge our responsibilities in obtaining basic scientific data for development purposes.
In this regard the hon. member for the Yukon, immediately after the words I have just read, went on:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Do you feel we have sufficient field laboratories in the north to accomplish the gathering of this scientific information?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, my opinion is that we do not have sufficient field laboratories. I do not want to imply that I support large research laboratories in the Arctic; I would sooner call them stations. I prefer small stations, because in due course one exhausts the scientific possibilities of an area. I do not think we have enough small scientific stations in the Arctic, stations to which scientists from various disciplines can go.
Then the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke asked Mr. Rowley what type of research they would carry on. He said that as he came from the south he did not understand the type of research that might be carried on in the Arctic. He asked Mr. Rowley what type of research would be carried on and Mr. Rowley answered:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I would like to see the stations concerned, first with the collection of what you might call the natural history of the area, and expanding that to the study of biology-the relationship between the animals and the vegetation, and I would also see the stations used as a basis from which investigations in other disciplines could be carried out-in archaeology and so on.
There is very little more in the evidence of the committee in this regard except that there were some questions about the depletion of the caribou and what scientific research might be done to indicate the reasons for this. There were also a few words about herding muskox, reindeer and buffalo, I think. Then there was a question about the Arctic institute of North America, and so on. But this is all the evidence that came before the committee on which the committee

made the sweeping recommendation that we find in its report. That is all the evidence we received. Only one witness was called. Although I agree with some parts of the report, I cannot agree with a sweeping recommendation such as this one made on the basis of the evidence we obtained. I do not think we have any evidence. As a matter of fact, I think that in most cases words were put in the witness' mouth and then written directly into the report in the same wording. As a matter of fact, it looks to me very much like a prearranged deal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, sir.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Was the hon. member on the steering committee of the mines, forests and waters committee?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You can sit down. No, sir.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Did the hon. member attend when the report of the committee was drafted?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I told the chairman that the report would be passed on division and that my support would not be recorded in favour of it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I merely asked if you were there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was there. I told the chairman. I am not going to go over the whole report but I should like to refer to section 28, paragraph (b), which reads as follows:
Your committee expresses concern that . . . the projects which are undertaken on the basis of past policies will result in the setting of standards which are unnecessarily high.
Then, section 29 reads as follows:
For instance, the standard of facility provided for the education of native northern children has been quite high. The hostel at Fort McPherson, the various buildings at Inuvik, and similar undertakings in other northern locations are examples in point.
I went through the evidence of the committee from one end to the other, Mr. Chairman, to find out on what they based this recommendation and how the hostel at Fort McPherson came into the picture. There was only one question in the whole of the evidence before the committee and that question was as to the cost of the Fort McPherson school. I forget the exact answer but I think it was something like $1,200,000. There was not another question. They did not know the size of the hostel, how many pupils there were, was there a playroom or an auditorium. They did not know how many cubic feet there 66968-9-372|
Supply-Northern Affairs were. There were no questions and no answers and yet they make this type of recommendation to the house.
As far as the buildings at Inuvik are concerned, there was no evidence given before the committee to justify this sort of sweeping statement. There is no evidence whatever. Look through the committee reports. I hope the minister will read them if he has not and tell us whether or not he agrees with the type of sweeping statement I have referred to in sections 24 and 25 and particularly in section 28.
I am not going to go through the rest of the report. I did not intend to take too much time on this matter but I want to point out that in my view the committee on mines, forests and waters had no right to bring in recommendations such as the ones to which I have just referred because there is no evidence in the committee reports to substantiate sweeping recommendations of that sort.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might, under this vote, inquire of the minister whether the Fraser river board has been reconstituted or if the cabinet has approved the re-establishment of the Fraser river board? Who are the personnel of the board, and what are the terms of reference, if that has been established by the cabinet?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if I could get some information from the minister concerning a statement that was made recently by Robert Moses, president of the New York state power authority. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In the first place, on a question of accuracy, the board
fMr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle).]

comes under the international joint commission; it is the St. Lawrence river board. The board reports to the minister of external affairs, but I am on the committee so I would have some knowledge of it.
The action we are taking is as I have described. We have formed a committee at cabinet and the official level and are negotiating with the government of Ontario.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the statement made by the chairman of the New York state power authority accurate?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask this additional question? I know that some of this is under the jurisdiction of other departments, but the minister said something about the Ontario agreement. I understand that the Ontario agreement is ineffective; is that the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is in effect.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to leave a couple of thoughts with the minister in so far as the operation of the Fraser river board is concerned, and particularly some of the material contained in the preliminary report on flood control which was issued in June of 1958. I imagine that this preliminary report, like the interim report before it and the appendices, have been very carefully studied not only by this department but other departments of government of both the federal and provincial governments involved. There appears to be one matter dealt with in the preliminary report that would warrant action being taken on the material contained therein without waiting another three or four years until

the board has completed its studies, as I understand it will take that length of time when the board is reconstituted.
In order to give some of the hon. members an understanding of the length of the area that is contained by the Fraser river, perhaps I could just say that it is over 800 miles in length and that it drains an area larger than the four maritime provinces put together. It is the most important fish river in British Columbia and one of the most important fish rivers in the world. This is one of the points of conflict in British Columbia at the moment and the federal government is involved. I refer to the fish versus power question, and whether or not dams should be placed on any of the tributaries to the Fraser or on any parts of the Fraser itself. However, I do not want to deal with the question of the hydroelectric-fish problem. We dealt with that question to some extent in the marine and fisheries committee. I should like to deal with the question of flood control.
Certainly British Columbia members who are here will recall the disastrous flood that took place in the Fraser valley in 1948 and along other rivers on the coast; but we recall the one in the Fraser valley which was the most disastrous and caused untold damage to farm lands and to buildings, to people's savings and to the very economy of the Fraser valley itself. In fact, the assessed value of the land and improvements in the Fraser valley that our now protected to a limited degree by the dikes that were established at the time of the 1948 flood is estimated or was actually in 1956 over $113 million, the market value of this land and improvements being somewhere in the neighbourhood, as the report of the board indicates, of $283 million. This report deals quite extensively with the question of flood control. It relates a number of alternate ways in which we can deal with flood control.
Before proceeding to what I think the report indicates is the most economical and fastest way to provide flood control protection for the Fraser valley I should like to point out that following the flood of 1948 the federal government and the provincial government entered into a joint financing of the diking plan along the Fraser valley, with the federal government paying 75 per cent of the cost and the provincial government putting up 25 per cent and they had completed that work in a period of a little less than two years. I believe it was a year and nine months or ten months that it took to complete the full diking that was necessary or that they felt was necessary at that time.
This preliminary report of the Fraser river board points out that it is possible to bring
Supply-Northern Affairs these dikes up to a standard which would contain what they estimate would be the highest possible runoff which they might expect based on past experience of floods and runoffs in that particular area and that this could be done at a cost of approximately $17 million, and that the operating cost of the dikes, maintenance and so on would cost another $1,195,000.
Another part of the report dealt with an alternate system of dikes and reservoirs further up the Fraser, that is dikes along the Fraser valley at the lower portion of it before it runs out into the gulf of Georgia; dikes there and reservoirs on tributaries and on streams further up inland-at an estimated cost of $526 million. What I am suggesting- and I rather think that the Fraser river board in its report suggests this too-is that if you are going to deal with the question of diking in order to protect the Fraser valley and $283 million worth of land and improvements, homes and farms of people throughout the valley and deal with the economy and protect the economy of the Fraser valley, the best way in which to do that is immediately to start planning to rebuild the dikes up to a level that will contain the flood level waters which they might expect to occur based on past experience of floods rather than attempt over a long period of time to put, as the report indicates, $526 million into reservoir dams and into diking also.
I am sure in my own mind that this government will not be less generous than was the former Liberal government preceding it. I believe it would want to be at least as generous and, if I am not mistaken, would want to go just one better; that is, if we can take account of what the Prime Minister has said in what my friend the . hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate classifies as his very modest manner. But the federal government I think should right now start, if they have not already done so, to discuss the question of the diking of the Fraser valley with the provincial authorities and agree to be as generous at least as was the past Liberal administration in going for 75 per cent of the cost of rebuilding these dikes and should attempt to enter into this sort of agreement with the province before it is too late. We could very easily find next spring-next May and next June, for instance-that we in the Fraser valley-and in other parts of the province but in the Fraser valley particularly because that is the one I am dealing with and this Fraser river board deals with that section

Supply-Northern Affairs -would be faced with something similar to the disastrous flood which occurred in the Fraser valley in 1948.
In my estimation it is far better to do as I have suggested. There is an old saying that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. That saying applies to the Fraser valley just as it applies to other things. The federal government should start off now, if it has not already done so, and approach the province and indicate its willingness to find at least the 75 per cent that the Liberal administration went for- at least that amount of the cost of rebuilding the dikes to withstand the flood levels which they expect might occur. That will be a great deal better than to wait and then, if we have a disastrous flood next spring, scurry around to try to find the money, to try to get men and equipment in order to build up dikes to try to contain the river and in the process do a rather haphazard job and have many of the farms and the homes and the community in the Fraser valley flooded out as they were in 1948.
I suggest that the minister should take this question as being one of paramount importance and requiring immediate action. The question of hydroelectric development and the possibility of maintaining the Fraser river as a fish river is one that does not require immediate action. We have other hydroelectric projects in the offing in British Columbia, one of which might be dealt with in the house. Undoubtedly my friend the hon. member for Kootenay West will take occasion to deal with the possibility of developing the Columbia.
Then there is this great area to the north, and so on, but that is something which is not of immediate importance as is the question of providing dikes to sufficiently high levels in the Fraser valley to protect the people who live there from being flooded out as they were in 1948. If the minister will undertake to engage in that sort of program I know he will not find any objection from the people in the Fraser valley, and certainly will not find any objection from myself or I am sure from any other hon. member who knows of the disaster brought upon the people in the Fraser valley in 1948 merely because governments prior to that time did not have foresight to see that floods could take place and practically wipe out the entire valley itself. Not only do I make this suggestion but the minister should start right now with a flood control program for the Fraser valley by participating with the province in diking. I would appreciate it if he would give the committee an indication of his attitude in this regard and tell us what action has been

taken, what studies have been made and what steps are under way to start such a program of diking and flood containment in the valley.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In view of the most important and most welcome speech of the hon. member, there must be some answer from the minister on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

All I can say is
that the two governments have agreed to study the report. As to the diking, they are a provincial responsibility, and all we are doing under these studies, as I see it, is trying to make arrangements to fix the boat instead of trying to bail it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is a pretty weak and a pretty poor answer and attitude for the minister to take. We realize that the province has agreed to reconstitute the board and study the question, but as sure as I am standing here, if the Fraser valley ends up being flooded out next year the words of the minister will come back to the people of the Fraser valley and they will not forget. The minister cannot pass the buck and say that diking is a provincial responsibility. In 1948 the minister's predecessor, whom he tries to outdo on every occasion, established the principle that it was a disaster area and that the federal government had a responsibility, and they supported their responsibility to the extent of 75 per cent of the cost.
There is a federal government responsibility in this field or you would not be involved in participating in the establishment of a board to study the question of flood control in the first place. You cannot wash your hands of it that easily especially if there is a flood. If you are gambling that there will not be a flood in the Fraser valley within the next three or four years, during which time this Fraser river board is supposed to meet and study further the question of hydroelectric power, fish runs and everything else, then I hope you win your gamble. But it will be your neck and your responsibility and your reputation, as well as the reputation of this federal government, which will be at stake. The last government indicated eleven years ago that there was a responsibility by paying part of the cost, and it will be the reputation of this government which will suffer, along with the suffering which will come to the people in the valley, if there is a flood. As I say, if you are gambling there will not be, I hope you win your bet, and that there will not be any flood; but I suggest that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure and

it is far better to be generous now, as was the case in 1948, than to follow your policy of re-establishing the board to discuss the question of flood control.
If the government has no responsibility, what is it doing in the field of studying this question in the first place? It would be far better off to follow that responsibility a little further and indicate its willingness to work with the provincial government. This can be done privately behind the scenes if you do not want any publicity attached to it, but the government should indicate its willingness to participate in the question of flood containment dikes along the Fraser valley. The reference to continuing to bail the boat out rather than fix it is an off the cuff comment which does not fit the circumstances at all.
If the minister looks at the report of the board he will see, so far as flood control is concerned, that diking is an integral part of any system. Even the reservoir program and the dikes themselves run to $526 million including $17 million for diking if brought up to a sufficiently high level, and it takes into account the question that it is necessary to build dikes rather than dams farther up the Fraser river. If the minister is indicating that he is in favour of building dams, hydroelectric reservoirs, storage and every other sort of project on the Fraser river, and in the process ruin the river as a fish run, then he had better talk to his colleague the Minister of Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would just like to get the record straight. The Fraser river board is, under the joint constitution of the two governments, trying to arrive at a plan to use the resources of the Fraser river without harm to the fishing industry and to protect the people along the banks against flooding, which includes diking, and also to provide enough power to pay for the whole operation. As I described it a moment ago, it is the firm opinion of the province of British Columbia that it is much better to get a policy which makes full use of the resources of the river without harming anybody else, and thereby, as I said earlier, fix the boat instead of just bailing here and there.
