speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Anything to oblige; a provincial park may be a natural resource.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think I must insist that we find out if there is any road to resources program in Ontario, where that is and how much money has been spent. I think this is information that we should have. I do not know where these roads are, but I understand there are some. I should like the minister to tell us where they are, the extent of these roads that have already been built under this program. I am not asking for confidential information on negotiations for proposed roads, but just roads that are either under construction or have been bruit under this program.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I can say this, that in Ontario there are seven roads upon which agreements have been made. There are two more that are under negotiation. I am not at liberty, under the agreement I have, to divulge them here until the agreement has been signed. There is only one exception to that. If any member asks about a specific road that has been agreed upon, I would acknowledge, yes or no, that that was it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Tell us now, then, what are the seven roads agreed upon, not the two under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I just finished saying that I cannot do so under the agreement I have with the province of Ontario.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister has just said he does not have any agreement with the province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This is a most extraordinary situation. There have been contracts agreed upon, money spent and roads built, but we are told this afternoon in this House of Commons that the minister cannot break a confidence and tell the committee of the money spent and the roads built. Will the minister explain why, with the taxpayers' money being spent, roads built, contracts fulfilled, he is not permitted, under a confidence, to tell this committee why or where the money was spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have made it very clear to the committee this afternoon there has been no money spent by the federal government under this agreement and there will not be until an agreement is signed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I thought you said seven had been built?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is one aspect of this, as I mentioned to the minister before, which is even more unfair than the point that has just been made. The effect of this program, in co-operation with the provinces, is that requests for information on the order paper have been denied. I am willing to concede that the minister, in confidence, has been willing to give us some information.
What is the situation on the provincial side? Can the minister explain to me why, if this is an agreement in confidence, the premier of Ontario and his disciples have been able in the last few months to range around the northern part of the province announcing these agreements in detail, even saying who was going to have the contract? This is the unfair side of it. This is where in fact it seems to me the minister has let the hon. member down. I should just like an explanation of it.
Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I feel that as long as I keep my part of the bargain I have done my duty. I cannot be held responsible for the leak or the use of the information that occurred in Ontario.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Let me just give an example of the context in which these announcements are made. I had one report from a political rally that said: "Look what you have. Now you have a Conservative government in Ottawa. If you re-elect a Conservative government in Ontario we are going to bring all these things to fruition". We cannot be blamed for taking a sort of jaundiced look at this particular kind of partisanship. I insist that if the hon. member for Port Arthur in the provincial constituency has the right, week after week, to make announcements about the building of a tiny culvert on one of these blasted roads on the roads to resources program, I as a member of this house should have the right to have some public information on the matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I want to support very warmly what has been said by the hon. member for Port Arthur. It is the most outrageous thing that I have heard said on the estimates in this house since I have been here. Here we are in the House of Commons of Canada being asked to vote money for a provincial purpose. The provincial government feels perfectly free in an election campaign to further its interests by broadcasting this information and we in the House of Commons are not entitled to be told, the minister says, because he has an agreement. Yet he tells us that he has not an agreement, that no agreement has been signed. He means that he reached some private understanding in his negotiations that he would not say anything about this matter until an agreement was reached.
We were very reasonable about the matter. Both the hon. member for Timiskaming and I said that if there was any road not yet in the program which they were still discussing, we would not imperil those discussions. But we know perfectly well that a great many of these roads have been agreed upon. Some of them have been started. One hon. member told me that one of the roads had work being done on it until the election and that no work has been done on it since then. I do hot know whether or not that is true but it would not surprise me. Yet here the people who are the trustees for the taxpayers who have to pay for these things cannot have any information about them. This is an absolutely preposterous situation. Of course the minister has a huge majority behind him. If he wants to treat parliament in that way,

Supply-Northern Affairs I suppose in the end we have to submit but at least we should protest about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this attitude of the opposition this afternoon, first of all by the hon. member for Mackenzie River and now once again by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, goes a little bit beyond what they can expect the minister to sit here and take. The dirty, vicious remarks this afternoon about Indians are now duplicated by a sneering, McCarthy-like statement by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Just because there is an information leak at the provincial level he stands up here and asks me to break my written word in letters to the governments of these provinces that no information would be put out from the federal level. If he is absolutely fair he will realize this. Conservative members from Prince Edward Island have come to me with complaints that they had no information about what Liberal M.L.A.'s in Prince Edward Island are doing with the roads program in their province. Why does not the hon. member apply the same rule of ethics to the Liberal government in Prince Edward Island?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I will answer that question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Just you sit down until I finish.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That's the stuff.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, I will not sit down until the hon. gentleman is finished.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was going to sit down but now I rise on a question of privilege. I had not intended to bother doing it but in view of the attitude of the hon. gentleman I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman talked about my upholding the rights of parliament as being McCarthy-like tactics. That is an improper imputation of motives which the hon. member has no right whatsoever to make. I will not take up the time of the committee by asking him to withdraw it because the country is soon going to discover what attention should be paid the remarks made by this hon. gentleman. However, I will say this about Prince Edward Island. If that is being done in Prince Edward Island, it is wrong also. We in parliament are entitled to know this. Why there should be such secrecy about where these roads are going to be anyway, I do not understand. When we sat over there on the other side and proposed to keep secret certain things about the armament program of this country we were accused-
IMr. Pickersgill.]

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not a question of privilege. The minister has the floor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I suggest the hon. member stick to the question of privilege.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: My question of privilege is that the minister has made a malicious attack upon my reputation and I am entitled to repudiate that attack. All I did which gave him any excuse for making that attack was to point out that parliament was entitled to information which provincial premiers and provincial cabinet ministers were spreading abroad about the country but which was denied us in this parliament. If that is McCarthyism, I intend to go on indulging in McCarthyism.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I gather that the chairman has ruled that there is no question of privilege.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was on my
feet with regard to inferences and allegations spread around by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. You can see, Mr. Chairman, the way in which his mind is twisted. I said that he was applying to one province's political party a code of ethics which was different from what he was willing to apply to another.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not say anything about any province.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then the hon. member is up like a firecracker and he tells us he is defending the rights of parliament. This afternoon, Mr. Chairman, this parliamentary institution, as we have known it, from the type of activities that have gone on the other side of the house, has taken a greater series of blows than it could sustain from any leaks or any misuse of information in the hands of provincial politicians. I should like nothing better, Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You should have been here in 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-than to give the name of every road and the amount that was spent on every road. I will give to this house all the information I have here available and put it on the record so you can go back and say that this is being done.
To those in British Columbia you can say that a road is being built under agreement 255 miles in length. The amount that was spent up to March 31, 1959 was $2,040,000. You can say in Alberta there is general agreement now on a road program for 430 miles of road and that all the province spent there up

to March 31, 1959 was $500,000. In Saskatchewan there is agreement as far as the actual roads are concerned on 824 miles of road. Work started on May 5, 1958, last year, and is still continuing. The province's expenditures to March 31, 1959 are $2,500,000. In Manitoba the agreement calls for 688 miles of road. They started work on May 28 last year. The expenditures up to March 31, are $1,500,000. In Ontario the agreement at the present time calls for 355 miles of road. The amount actually spent up to March 31, 1959 was $200,000. When I hear here of all these roads starting and stopping after election time may I say that there could not have been too much there under this program because that is all we spent on this program.
In New Brunswick the agreement calls for 417 miles of road. They did $1,500,000 worth of work last year. In Nova Scotia the agreement calls for 465 miles of road and $2,500,000 was spent last year. In Prince Edward Island, 343 miles of road-on that little island-and they spent $2,500,000 last year. In Newfoundland, 269 miles of road so far have been agreed upon and they spent $220,000 last year. The total amount spent last year up to March 31, 1959 was $12,960,000. The amounts that we will have to pay can be easily discovered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that they spent $2,500,000 in Prince Edward Island? I thought the limit for each province was $1,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The limit each year in a province is $3 million, of which we pay one-half, $1,500,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And $2,500,000 was spent in Prince Edward Island last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is the
figure I have here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The information given us by the minister is most interesting and we appreciate it. We are now discussing this afternoon the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1960. The minister was most interesting, yes and informative, but I want to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that we are discussing now vote 280, which is the contribution to the provinces to assist in the development of roads leading to resources in accordance wtih agreements entered into by Canada and the provinces, and for that, in the period starting April 1 of this year until March 31 of next year, the minister is asking for the sum of $9 million. That is not for something in the past but for something in the future.
Supply-Northern Affairs
The only answer we have had from the minister so far is: "It is confidential; I cannot break confidences." Mr. Chairman, I say that if the members of this House of Commons are being asked to give authority for the payment of $9 million, then we are entitled to know where and why this $9 million is going to be spent. It is not good enough for us to wait until next year when the money has been spent. We have the authority now to decide whether the money shall be spent or not and I say that it is positively disgusting and disgraceful that the minister hides himself under the cloak that he has secret agreements with provinces and cannot tell the House of Commons, which has to pass the money, how, where or why the money will be spent.
Mr. Chairman, surely that is something that no one in this house should be entitled to anticipate or expect and as a matter of fact I have not even yet got the answer to the question I asked previously as to how it ties in with roads. But the important thing is this. The minister almost had a halo around his head when he told us how the money was spent last year. We are not discussing how the money was spent last year. That is a matter of public accounts and concerns the public accounts committee. What we have before us now is not the public accounts of last year but the estimates for the next 12 months, and under vote 280 we are being asked for $9 million. The minister has not told us one word yet. He has not taken us into his confidence one iota, except to say that he cannot because it is confidential with the provinces. Mr. Chairman, you may have something in common with the provinces and you may have some secret agreements, but it is the House of Commons which has to pass this $9 million and we are entitled to know how, why and where that $9 million is going to be spent. Until I get that answer I will have to reserve my opinion whether I vote for it or not because I want to know where, how and why this money is going to be spent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am not at all satisfied with the answer we got. I do not see why this should be secret in the first place, and I think it is high time the people of Ontario who have heard a great deal about access roads finally discovered where those access roads are. We have had an unpleasant record in Ontario with roads under a Conservative government, roads which were never built that we passed money for, particularly the bridge sections of those roads. I do not think that a federal Conservative government will be any better than a provincial Conservative government was, and I think parliament has the right to know

Supply-Northern Affairs where these particular roads are so that we can see if they are roads which are worth while or not. This seems to me a wonderful way of passing out patronage between the province and the federal government, when you do not have to explain where there is a road or there is not a road. We have to take the minister's word that there are 335 miles already contracted for in Ontario and that we have already spent some $200,000. He did not give us the figures for the ones which were not contracted for, I suppose because we did not ask for them.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that these roads have to serve some purpose, and they cannot serve a purpose unless they are known to the people in the communities nearby. I think we should point out to the minister that this $9 million in this particular item is not only in this year but was in last year. There is no difference between the item this year as compared with last year. I am not familiar with the geographical situation in the province of Prince Edward Island, but it always seemed to me that it was a fairly small province and I am surprised to find that $2,500,000 was spent in looking for the resources in that province. It indicates to me that there is probably not the supervision of this program that the minister envisioned for the Canadian people when he talked about it in the first place.
A great deal was said about these resource roads in the recent provincial election in the province of Ontario. At that time in various ridings there was reference to roads being built in the next riding, but there was no reference to the ones in my particular riding. I heard of roads which were going to be built from Timmins to Kapuskasing and other roads going to be built in numerous places, and I think we are entitled to this information and we are going to demand that it be made available to the committee. If not I will be quite happy to talk on this item until six o'clock and the minister can think it over during the weekend.
We are very much in favour of this roads to resources program. We know there are many areas in our part of the country in northern Ontario that have not been developed, and one of the reasons they have not been developed is that we have not been able to get roads put into those particular areas. In the province of Ontario the department of mines has gone into highway construction. Throughout northern Ontario they are building various sections of highways which the department of highways usually take over after they are completed.


I had hoped that this would be the same type of program that would happen under this particular vote.
I can envision many roads being constructed, and I want to refer to one of them, the road from Kowganda and Shining Tree, West Tree, into the area of Sultan in the Chapleau district. This road is already completed and about 80 or 100 miles is owned by the K.P.C. The Kalamazoo Parchment Company have a big business in that area and they built a road at their own expense and closed it off to traffic, with the exception of the vehicles of some private individuals who have permission from the company to go through. This is a very important road because it opens up that new area in Kowganda, which is a well developed mining area.
This would mean that the tourist traffic, particularly from the area of Sault Ste. Marie and other areas would be greatly stimulated because of the benefit which would arise through having this important area of our country opened up to the public and made available for industrial development. I should like to know what consideration has been given to the roads which, we heard a year ago, were the only ones in which the minister was going to take an interest, that is those along the north branch of the Canadian National Railways. I was surprised, I must say, to hear that some of these roads were being built in places such as the province of Prince Edward Island-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if, in an effort to save the time of the committee, I could intervene at this point by reminding the committee that I said that if any hon. member asked me about a road that was approved I could tell him whether or not that was the case. The hon. member has mentioned a road, and I can tell him that the road which he has mentioned was proposed by the Ontario government and approved.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am willing to accept that. The minister has given me the information as it affects a constituency, but it was information given to me in confidence. The fact remains that other parties had not treated it in confidence. Surely if you have a deal and they do not keep one aspect of it, you can do something about it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the way you would operate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare says: "That is the way you would operate." So this is a fine way to operate, is it? We have got a sunshine blowhard up

at the lakehead who announces every culvert and bridge crossing that comes along and he has been announcing them for months in connection with the roads to resources program, and I consider it an insult to the House of Commons that he should be announcing federal jobs. This affects other departments of government, and the situation produces its ridiculous aspects when you have a situation arising where a minister of defence production is unwilling to give information on particular questions addressed to him while this sunshine blowhard is spreading the information up there. All this party understanding business on the provincial and federal level depresses me. This is the sort of thing I could get very annoyed about- and I do not often get annoyed-because it involves the dignity of members of this house -I don't care whether they are Conservatives, Liberals or members of the C.C.F. I admit that the minister in this regard has been fair with me, within the limits that he has announced. I have been able to go to his office and get the information. But this is a damnable situation, and one to which I object very strongly. I suggest that an hon. member has the right to know if a contract has been broken-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the hon.
member will take my word for it, I will call the premier and ask permission to forget this mutual understanding of the two governments, though, no doubt, that will cause some embarrassment in other provinces. I will certainly phone the premier, and I am quite certain that if it is correct that the information is around the province he would agree that there is no reason to keep it quiet. The election is over.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is the answer.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What a horrible admission. "The election is over". How little use some ministers have for the rights of parliament when they can make that kind of statement. That makes it even worse-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we had better have some order brought into this committee. I am speaking on a point of order. I gave an answer to the hon. member and in giving that answer I stated quite candidly that I could not see there was any reason whatever of a political nature-there was no election in the offing -for not giving this information and immediately this stampede starts. My point of order is this: if we are going to conduct this committee of estimates, we have to decide whether we are going to have information about my department or whether we are going to fight a political battle in this committee.
Business of the House
I think you should decide whether the type of stuff that has been going on this afternoon is in order or not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On the point of order which has been raised, I cannot understand a man in the position of the minister of northern affairs suggesting that the remarks that have been made are remarks which should not be made by a member of parliament. We have heard the word "McCarthyism" hurled back and forth across this floor this afternoon. This would suggest to me that the minister is not only hurling the accusation, but also trying to practise it. The minister has said now: "We shall make this information available; why not? The election is over." What a slur on the House of Commons, that we should now get information because an election is over.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have the floor on a point of order and I refuse to sit down for the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Kindly
address the Chair.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a fine remark. I was speaking on a point of order when I was rudely interrupted by the minister of northern affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am rising on a question of privilege.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, you cannot have a point of order and a question of privilege at the same time. Now, on the point of order-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I want a ruling on this question regarding a point of order and a point of privilege.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Six o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It
being six o'clock I do now rise and report progress.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a question that I wish to bring to your attention.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: The business of the house has been terminated, though a discussion on the business of the following day is usually permitted.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
This is on the business of the house. A situation occurred in the committee and the question was raised with the deputy chairman as to whether or not a question of privilege could be raised on a point of

Business of the House
order. I would like you as Speaker to give a direction, not perhaps now but at the next sitting.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will state his point then.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask the minister who is leading the house what the business will be for all of next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was given to understand that some agreement had been reached among the whips of the parties and with the house leader with regard to attempting to terminate the business next week, on the understanding that we would complete the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources today and perhaps those of trade and commerce; but because of the developments that have occurred, I think all I can reasonably do at the present time is announce the government order of business for Monday.
The first item will be No. 12 on today's order paper having to do with grants to the province of Newfoundland. The second item will be No. 1 on today's order paper having to do with an extension of long term mortgage credit to farmers; No. 3 will be No. 11 on today's order paper, the resolution to approve the international wheat agreement; No. 4 will be No. 9 on today's order paper, the resolution with regard to approving the convention on the nationality of married women; No. 5 will be No. 7 on today's order paper, the second reading of Bill No. S-25, to confirm an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Nova Scotia; No. 6 will be No. 4 on today's order paper, a somewhat similar agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the province of New Brunswick; and No. 7 will be the second reading of Bill No. S-2, to amend the Public Lands Grant Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask the leader of the house what estimates will be taken up next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it would be advisable now to await the return of the house leader who apparently had some discussion with members on the other side as to the business for next week. We have his suggestions already with regard to estimates. I presume they would be taken in this order, the completion of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, followed by trade and commerce; then, mines and technical surveys; national health and welfare, fisheries, post office, secretary of state, privy council, national revenue, legislation and finance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask what we shall do on Tuesday in case the items that were mentioned were completed on Monday?

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I understand legislation will be the last?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having announced the business for Monday, in the present circumstances I think that is as far as I should go. The house leader will give the announcement on Monday night.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: If we do not complete the business mentioned for Monday will we go on with that business on Tuesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Oh, yes, and with any other bills that have not been dealt with. For example, the first item on Monday will be the resolution on the grants to Newfoundland. If that passes, then second reading of that would follow on Tuesday. I think the legislative program I have announced might well consume the two days' time.
It being eight minutes past six o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to the order of the house passed on June 25.

CHANGING OF GUARD, PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government been requested to choose members of the armed forces, rather than those of our illustrious Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to carry out the daily changing of the guard in front of the parliament buildings?
2.	If so, by whom were such requests made, and on what occasion?
3.	Has the government decided to establish this British tradition permanently in Canada?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of
National Defence):
1, 2 and 3. As on previous occasions, a military guard was mounted on government house during the residence of Her Majesty the Queen. Following a number of requests, including representations from the Ottawa board of trade, arrangements were made to continue this practice during the summer months and to carry out the ceremony of the changing of this guard, which is a traditional ceremonial drill of the Canadian army, on the lawns in front of the parliament buildings.
It is not the practice for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to undertake this type of ceremony.
